title: Capital Maritime Finance Corp. (CMF): A New Chapter for Greek Shipping Capital Markets
summary: Capital Maritime Finance Corp. (CMF) is entering the market with a new container fleet, heavily marketed on its "latest-generation" and "energy-efficient designs," including LNG dual-fuel and CII Grade A vessels. Dirtiestships.com remains highly skeptical of such "green" claims, as methane slip from LNG remains a significant emissions concern. We will rigorously monitor CMF's operational carbon intensity to ensure these vessels consistently meet their ambitious CII targets and avoid FuelEU Maritime fines, rather than just relying on design specifications.
content:
Capital Maritime Finance Corp. (CMF), backed by Greek shipowner and investor Evangelos Marinakis, is preparing to enter the Athens Stock Exchange with a modern container fleet, long-term contracted revenues and an ambitious newbuilding programme — offering investors exposure to one of the fastest-evolving segments of global shipping.

The planned listing of CMF on the Athens Stock Exchange (Euronext Athens) marks another step in the expansion of the Capital Maritime Group’s presence in the international capital markets.

More importantly, it comes at a time when the container shipping industry is undergoing a profound transformation. Fleet renewal, environmental regulation, energy efficiency and the changing structure of global supply chains are reshaping the economics of the sector.

Against this backdrop, CMF is building its proposition around three core pillars: a young and technologically advanced fleet, long-term contracted revenues and access to a significant pipeline of new tonnage.

A Fleet Built for the Next Cycle

At the core of CMF’s investment proposition is a fleet of 36 latest-generation container vessels, comprising 13 vessels already in operation and a further 23 under construction.

The combined fleet will provide more than 148,000 TEU of capacity. Upon completion of the current delivery programme, its TEU-weighted average age is expected to be approximately two years, placing CMF among the youngest fleets in the international container shipping sector.

The composition of the fleet also reflects the industry’s accelerating transition towards greater energy efficiency and lower emissions.

CMF’s vessels include LNG dual-fuel tonnage, while the fleet incorporates energy-efficient designs achieving CII Grade A and vessels capable of connecting to shore power. These characteristics are increasingly relevant as environmental regulation becomes a more significant factor in fleet deployment, chartering decisions and long-term asset values.

For CMF, fleet renewal is therefore not simply a question of age. It is also intended to provide greater flexibility as regulatory requirements and customer expectations continue to evolve.

Visibility in a Volatile Market

One of the defining features of CMF’s business model is the extent of its contracted revenue base.

The company has $3.9 billion in secured revenues, with 100% of the fleet’s available days contracted through 2034. The average remaining charter duration stands at 9.5 years.*

*As of 30 June 2026.

In an industry traditionally exposed to pronounced freight-rate cycles, such a level of forward coverage provides a substantial degree of earnings visibility.

The company’s chartering relationships include global supply-chain players such as CMA CGM and DP World/Unifeeder, reinforcing its exposure to established counterparties in the container shipping market.

Three Generations of Shipping Experience

Behind the fleet and the balance sheet is a shipping organisation whose experience spans three generations.

For CMF, the combination of long-standing sector expertise and a professionally managed operating platform is central to its proposition. In an industry where commercial timing, fleet management and capital allocation can have a material impact on returns, accumulated shipping knowledge remains an important competitive asset.

The company’s strategy is therefore built not only around the acquisition and deployment of modern tonnage, but also around the experience required to navigate the industry’s cycles.

A $1.8 Billion Investment Programme

CMF’s growth strategy extends beyond its existing fleet.

The company is pursuing an investment programme of approximately $1.8 billion through 2028, primarily supporting a substantial newbuilding programme and providing a pipeline for further fleet growth.

The scale and timing of this investment are significant. Container shipping has entered a period in which owners are having to balance the replacement of older tonnage with increasingly stringent environmental requirements, while also assessing the long-term implications of alternative fuels and changing trade patterns.

CMF’s orderbook is designed to position the company within that transition rather than behind it.

An Income Proposition for Investors

Alongside fleet growth, CMF intends to offer investors a clearly defined distribution policy.

The company aims to distribute a stable portion of adjusted net income to shareholders on a quarterly basis, creating an income component alongside the potential for capital appreciation associated with the growth of the fleet.

The combination of contracted revenues, a young fleet and a sizeable orderbook is intended to provide a degree of earnings visibility that is unusual in a highly cyclical industry.

Building on Capital Maritime’s Listed Track Record

CMF’s planned listing follows the capital-markets trajectory of other companies associated with the Capital Maritime Group.

Capital Clean Energy Carriers and Capital Tankers have a combined market capitalisation of more than $4 billion.

Capital Clean Energy Carriers

Capital Clean Energy Carriers has established one of the largest modern LNG shipping platforms among U.S.-listed companies, with:

32 LNG/LPG vessels

Approximately $2.9 billion in contracted revenue backlog

77 consecutive quarterly dividend distributions

The largest modern LNG carrier fleet among U.S.-listed shipping companies

€500 million raised through three unsecured bond issues in the Greek market

Figures as of 30 June 2026.

Capital Tankers

Capital Tankers added another international capital-markets milestone in 2026 with its listing on Euronext Growth Oslo.

The transaction included:

A $500 million IPO

Listing in the first quarter of 2026

A 39.9% increase in the share price during the first six months of trading, from NOK 134 to NOK 187.5*

*Through 17 September 2026.

The experience of these companies provides CMF with an established reference point as it approaches the Greek capital market.

Evangelos Marinakis and the Capital Markets Strategy

The planned CMF listing also forms part of a broader strategy pursued by Evangelos Marinakis, founder and Chairman of Capital Maritime & Trading Corp.

The Capital Maritime Group currently manages a fleet of 179 vessels, including the fleets of Capital Clean Energy Carriers, Capital Tankers and the newly established CMF.

Marinakis has more than 20 years of experience in the international capital markets, during which companies backed by him have completed major IPOs and corporate transactions, including two significant U.S. mergers, while also raising capital through three successful bond issues in Greece.

Since 2007, listed shipping companies backed by Marinakis have distributed more than $1 billion in dividends to shareholders.

In 2025, Lloyd’s List ranked Marinakis 10th in its annual list of the 100 most influential people in global shipping. In 2024, he received an Honorary Doctorate from the Massachusetts Maritime Academy, while since 2022 he has served as an elected member of the Board of the Union of Greek Shipowners.

Beyond Shipping

Marinakis is also the founder and principal shareholder of Alter Ego Media, one of Greece’s leading Media & Entertainment groups and one of the fastest-growing integrated media platforms in Southern Europe.

Following its listing on the Athens Stock Exchange in 2025, Alter Ego Media recorded a 57.5% share price return, compared with a 37% return for the General Index. Its IPO raised approximately €57 million in gross proceeds and was nearly 12 times oversubscribed, with total demand reaching approximately €677 million from retail and institutional investors.

Beyond his business interests, Marinakis supports a range of philanthropic initiatives in Greece and internationally, including UNICEF, the Miltiadis Marinakis Chair for Modern Greek Language and Culture at The Ohio State University, the Kazantzakis Museum in Crete, as well as social and infrastructure projects in Piraeus and elsewhere in Greece.

A Shipping Platform for the Next Decade

CMF’s proposed entry to the Athens Stock Exchange comes at the intersection of two developments: the transformation of the global container fleet and the growing role of Greek capital markets in financing internationally focused shipping companies.

Its proposition is built around a young fleet, long-term charter coverage, a substantial orderbook and the capital-markets experience of the wider Capital Maritime Group.

For investors, the attraction lies in the combination of contracted cash flows and fleet growth. For the Greek market, the listing would add another internationally focused shipping company to a capital market seeking to strengthen its position as a financing centre for global maritime businesses.

title: Shipping rewinds the future
summary: Ocean Network Express (ONE) is adopting "backcasting" to strategize for 2050, a theoretical planning exercise that risks sidestepping immediate, tangible commitments to decarbonization. While useful for long-term vision, this approach provides no concrete details on how ONE will reduce current carbon intensity or phase out heavy fuel oil (HFO) usage. Real progress demands immediate action to meet FuelEU Maritime targets and improve current CII ratings, not just future projections.
content:
Rather than forecasting from today, backcasting starts with possible futures and works backwards — an approach gaining traction as shipping’s long-term bets become harder to call. Splash’s Europe Editor Bojan Lepic explains.

Shipping has never been short on forecasts. Fleet growth, trade demand, freight rates, fuel choices, and asset values are all projected years ahead, even though the industry has a habit of making long-range predictions look fragile.

A different planning technique is now gaining attention. Rather than starting with today’s market and projecting forward, backcasting begins with a future scenario and works backwards to establish what needs to happen to get there.

Japanese liner Ocean Network Express (ONE) has brought the concept into sharper focus through its View of the World project, which examines several possible versions of the global economy and container shipping in 2050 and considers what those futures mean for decisions made today. The carrier examines how long-lived investments such as ships and terminals fit across different scenarios rather than relying on a single projection of how the market develops.

A spokesperson for ONE stresses that the exercise is not designed to produce another forecast.

“Backcasting is one of several strategic frameworks ONE uses, and we apply it as a planning discipline rather than a prediction tool. We set out multiple plausible scenarios for how the global economy and container shipping could look in 2050, drawing on a wide range of external and internal perspectives. By backcasting from that future, we can determine the strategic actions we must take today.”

The idea is not new. Governments and international organisations already use variations of backcasting. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development incorporates it into strategic foresight work, the UN Development Programme includes it in its strategic planning toolkit, while the UK government and Singapore’s Centre for Strategic Futures use versions of the technique in public-sector planning.

“So backcasting has already caught on, but for long-range planning rather than within the current business cycle,” he tells Splash. “As ships are 25-30 year lifespan assets, backcasting can be a useful tool for strategic planning for ship owners investigating what the net zero world of 2050, or later, will look like.”

A conventional forecast might extrapolate container demand and calculate the fleet required to meet it. Backcasting can, for example, start with a competitive net-zero liner network in 2050 without a radically different pattern of world trade and work backwards through the ships, fuels, terminals, and technology required in 2045, 2040, and 2035.

Williams sees an advantage in escaping assumptions embedded in today’s market but also identifies one of the method’s central weaknesses.

“The danger of backcasting is that it can induce wishful thinking,” Williams says. “Circumstances outside your control can emerge over the backcasting period, so the backcast needs constant revision. Say, teleportation, for argument’s sake, is discovered, and shipping of inorganic objects becomes unnecessary. Or a future in which the human population peaks much earlier than currently expected. That could affect demand for container shipping, dry bulk shipping, and liquid fuel shipping.”

Tristan Smith, professor of energy and transport at the UCL Energy Institute, sees merit in the concept but says its usefulness depends on the futures being tested.

Katsuhiro Nishinari, professor at the University of Tokyo, is more bullish.

“Backcasting is a powerful methodology, especially in rapidly changing and highly uncertain environments like global shipping. Traditional forecasting tends to extrapolate current trends, which often fail when disruptive changes occur,” Nishinari says. He has been helping ONE with its backcasting project.

Nishinari does not see the technique replacing forecasting entirely but expects it to become more relevant as shipping deals with decarbonisation and other structural changes.

“While it requires a mindset shift and cannot completely replace traditional forecasting, backcasting is extremely useful for long-term strategic planning, particularly in areas like sustainability and decarbonisation. As companies face unprecedented future challenges, I believe more industries will adopt this approach,” he says.

Mikael Lind, senior strategic research advisor at RISE, sees another application: using backcasting to coordinate a fragmented maritime ecosystem.

“I do think backcasting has considerable potential in shipping, although I would not primarily see it as a better way of predicting the future,” Lind says, adding: “Backcasting means starting with a desired future and working backwards to identify what must happen to achieve it. That is fundamentally different from forecasting, where we start from where we are today and ask where current trends may take us.”

This matters because shipowners cannot deliver many of shipping’s biggest transitions alone. New fuels require producers and bunkering infrastructure. Ports require investment. Cargo owners, banks, regulators, shipyards, and technology providers all influence whether a future shipping system is achievable.

“This is where I think backcasting becomes particularly powerful. If the actors concerned jointly define a desired future state around a common object of interest, they can then work backwards together to identify what needs to be in place to reach it,” Lind says.

Shipping finance may already contain more backcasting than the industry realises, as Christopher Rex, head of innovation and research at Danish Ship Finance, points out.

“Backcasting will catch on, but it should not be sold as a better way of predicting shipping markets. It answers a different question. A forecast asks what is likely to happen,” Rex explains. “Backcasting asks what would have to be true for a given future to arrive, and what that implies for decisions taken today. For an industry that commits capital to ships trading well into the 2050s, that discipline is valuable.”

Rex says the Poseidon Principles trajectories effectively work backwards from the IMO’s 2050 ambition into annual carbon-intensity pathways. But a critical limitation remains for an industry where timing determines investment returns.

“The limitation is timing,” Rex argues. “Backcasting tells you where the industry is heading and which ships risk becoming unfinanceable before the end of their economic life. It says nothing about when to buy, at what price or with how much leverage, and in shipping, that is where most capital is made or lost.”

As is noticeable, backcasting has many positives, and some believe it is a potent tool in the shipping toolbox for building a clearer picture of the future. Others are more sceptical.

Kate Adamson, one of shipping’s best-known futurists, argues that the technique belongs to an earlier era of strategic planning.

“I’m afraid the 1990s just called and would like its scenario planning tool back. Backcasting has been around for decades, used by companies whose preferred future involved up-and-to-the-right growth in a VUCA – volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous – world.”

Adamson argues today’s environment is instead brittle, anxious, non-linear, and incomprehensible, making the starting assumptions behind any long-term exercise particularly vulnerable.

“Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face,” she quips. “The ones who will get back up are currently prioritising resilience, agility, adaptability, and continuity, not another buzzword.”

Nick Gross, Lloyd Register’s global containership segment director, takes a more measured position.

“Shipping has always relied on a range of tools to help navigate uncertainty, and backcasting is one of several approaches that organisations may choose to incorporate into their strategic planning,” he tells Splash.

Gross says its value depends heavily on the assumptions underpinning the scenario, while geopolitics, technology and economic shocks can quickly change shipping’s trajectory.

“For this reason,” he says, “we would not view backcasting as a substitute for forecasting or other forms of scenario analysis. Rather, it is one tool among many that can help support decision-making.”

That thinking is already visible among major shipmanagers.

Bjorn Hojgaard, chief executive of Anglo-Eastern, told the recent Splash Singapore event that the biggest strategic change is accepting that forecasting itself is becoming less dependable.

“It’s less about predicting the future and more about asking what we need to have in place in order to have optionality and cater to different futures,” he said.

Anglo-Eastern has run a long-range scenario exercise, working backwards from two very different versions of 2035 rather than trying to identify one future and plan exclusively around it.

That may be where backcasting ultimately finds its place in shipping. Few proponents argue that it can tell an owner what freight rates will be in five years, what a vessel will be worth at the bottom of the next cycle, or which fuel wins the race to replace conventional bunkers. Instead, it offers a way to test today’s long-lived investments against several possible tomorrows.

title: From Residue to Resource – the Rise and Risks of Marine Biofuels
summary: Despite buzz around bio-residue 'drop-in' fuels, 89.8% of the global fleet remains locked into oil-fired propulsion, ensuring continued reliance on fossil fuels. FuelEU Maritime's "surplus" credit system primarily serves as a financial workaround, allowing operators to buy their way out of fines rather than genuinely cutting carbon intensity. This policy risks perpetuating HFO usage under a veneer of decarbonization, delaying urgent, real emissions reductions.
content:
By Mark Smith, Director – Decarbonisation, NorthStandard

While corn, sugarcane, wheat, or vegetable oils can be converted into fuel, their use for foodis driving demand to develop waste or bi-products from agricultural, forestry, food-processing and other biological industries as more prudent alternatives. Bio-residues can, for example, be used to derive fuels or fuel blends which promise to ‘drop-in’ as replacements for conventional oils to help ships reduce greenhouse gas emissions (GHGs).

Already, Fuel EU Maritime regulations financially incentivise the use of bio-residue, where areduced emissions ‘surplus’ can be sold to ship operators in deficit to avoid compliance penalties.

A proposed revision to the EU ETS would introduce a technology neutral framework called SMAP (Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion) to help close the cost gap between fossil and low-carbon fuels.

Furthermore, the Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) encourages the production of biofuel from residues including used cooking oil (UCO), some animal fat, Palm Oil Mill Effluent, tall oil (a pine wood pulp by-product), and lignocellulosic residues (from non-food plant parts), as well as forestry, agricultural and some industrial residues

In its initial form, the IMO Net Zero Framework (NZF) also envisaged ‘GHG pricing’, supported by a mechanism incentivising lower emissions, although administrations are currently divided on whether the measure is workable, or even desirable. Between 30 November and 3 December, the 85th Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting willtest the basis on which the NZF can move forward.

Residual fuel demand

Nevertheless, demand for marine biofuels continues to grow. In its latest ‘Maritime Forecast to 2050’, DNV notes that 89.8% of in-service tonnage can operate only on oil fuels.

“This implies reliance on drop-in fuels such as fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) or hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) for decarbonization, unless these vessels are converted to use alternative fuels or equipped with onboard carbon capture and storage,” says DNV. “For vessels currently on order, 60.6% of the tonnage and 79.5% of the ships by number face similar limitations.”

Against this backdrop, it is likely that suppliers seeking to satisfy maritime demand will increasingly look beyond conventional feedstocks towards more complex bio-residuesources.

It is therefore worth acknowledging that bio-residues need to be treated as waste-derived fuelwhich require enhanced fuel-quality management and pollution preparedness.

Potential unintended consequences

As RED III applies to all industries, there will also be competition from the airline and heavy transport industries in the use of bio-residues, and we suspect this will create additional risksin the maritime sector.

Buyers in the sector may be exposed to lower-quality residues, for example, chemically variable feedstocks and/or blends from multiple residue streams. Pressure may mount on traceability systems, fraud risks may increase (due to misclassification of sustainabilityvalues in Proof of Compliance documents) and disputes over the chain of custodyaccumulate.

For ship operations, the risks may translate into oxidation instability, and greater variability in acidity and cold flow properties, or in degradation during storage. Lower quality fuels could foul injectors or cause fuel pump wear. More sediment could form and more blockages occur in purifiers and filters, and microbial growth could increase where residual contaminants or water are present.

Compatibility with conventional marine fuels and cross-contamination may also become issues when biofuel specifications are not reliable. Fuel incompatibility can cause issues with seals, gaskets, coatings and certain alloy metals.

Inconsistency in fuel composition between batches also has consequences for ship performance – during a single voyage and for the machinery condition over time. Uncertaintyover long-term engine performance could easily result in higher maintenance costs.

LossPreventionand bio-residues

Given the rising uptake of biofuels and the consequent risks, NorthStandard is recommending particular care in this area of marine fuel management. Members are advised to ensure that stringent tank cleaning requirements are upheld prior to use, for example.

Where standard fuel testing may not include parameters such as microbial growth, chemical contamination or other contaminants, NorthStandard recommends its Members consult fuel testing agencies for enhanced testing specific for biofuels.

General guidance to use reliable suppliers and require detailed fuel specifications and quality declarations is also supplemented by specific advice to avoid blending with other fuels unlesscompatibility testing confirms suitability. The P&I Club’s members can also use VPS fuel insights to check ISO Grade categorised data, but also the most common off-spec biofuel parameters, the suppliers with most ISO 8217 off specs at barge level and the ports with most off-spec fuels, among other information.

A general NorthStandard recommendation to minimise fuel storage duration is also augmented by counsel to undertake additional monitoring including temperature and water drainage, and to closely monitor purification, filtration, sludge production and fuel transfer system for abnormalities. Owners should also consider enhanced monitoring of fuel pumps, injectors and cylinder condition

Users of fuels derived from bio-residues should also ensure that their transfer procedures, spill contingency plans, Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP) and crew training are wholly suitable. They will also need to obtain and retain fuel composition documentation, including any blend information, as this will help with potential pollution clean-up actions for any properties that may disperse differently.

To ensure that uncertified products have not entered the supply chain, specific attention should also be given to certification such as the widely used International Sustainability & Carbon Certification ISSC EU. The right documentation is essential as proof that a biofuel is made from waste or residue as opposed to crops, to verify life cycle GHGs and to support 3rdparty compliance audits.

title: Why maritime decarbonisation matters for Australia
summary:
Australia’s economy and way of life depend on shipping.

Around 99% of Australia’s trade by volume and 87% by value is carried by sea, making maritime transport essential to the nation’s economic pros...
content:
Australia’s economy and way of life depend on shipping.

Around 99% of Australia’s trade by volume and 87% by value is carried by sea, making maritime transport essential to the nation’s economic prosperity and connection to global markets. At the same time, international shipping is beginning a major transition toward zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and technologies, driven by evolving regulation, customer expectations, and supply chain decarbonisation commitments.

Australia’s shipping-related greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from commodity exports are estimated at around 34 million tonnes annually, equivalent to approximately 8% of the country’s total GHG emissions. Although these emissions are not directly captured within Australia’s domestic emissions targets or policy framework, the Australian economy remains highly exposed to shipping’s net-zero transition.

Maritime decarbonisation is therefore not simply a climate issue, but an economic, energy security, and strategic opportunity for Australia.

As key trading partners such as Japan, South Korea, and China move to reduce emissions across global supply chains, Australia’s competitiveness will increasingly be influenced by the emissions performance of the products it exports and the systems used to transport them.

Australia’s resources and energy exports are forecast to generate more than AUD $400 billion in export earnings in 2026-27, with iron ore alone accounting for more than a quarter of those earnings. Supporting the uptake of clean maritime fuels can help ensure Australia remains integrated into the low-emission supply chains being developed by its major trading partners. It will also help maintain the international competitiveness of key export industries, including iron ore, critical minerals, agriculture, aluminium, and other energy-intensive sectors. At the same time, it will reinforce Australia’s reputation as a reliable trading partner in a low-carbon global economy.

As these trading partners pursue green steel, low-emissions manufacturing, and broader industrial decarbonisation pathways, demand for lower-emission commodities and supply chains is expected to grow. Shipping could provide one of the earliest sources of demand for alternative fuels such as ammonia, helping unlock investment in fuel production, storage, transport, and bunkering infrastructure. Realising this opportunity will require coordinated policy, investment, and industry action to scale the fuel production and supporting infrastructure needed to provide confidence for private investment.

Concentrated export hubs and shipping routes—such as those supporting Australia’s iron ore exports—offer practical opportunities to aggregate demand, demonstrate commercial viability, and support the growth of Australia’s emerging clean fuel industry.

The energy security opportunity

There is also a compelling energy security rationale. Australia remains heavily dependent on imported fuels, with approximately 95% of its transport fuels sourced from overseas. This leaves the economy exposed to the impacts of international supply disruptions, price shocks, and geopolitical uncertainty on the cost and availability of conventional maritime fuel.

Australia also has limited domestic capability to produce fossil maritime fuels, as remaining crude oil resources are scarce and internationally uncompetitive. By contrast, Australia has abundant low-cost renewable energy potential and diverse sources of low-emissions biomass, creating an opportunity to develop domestic production of hydrogen, ammonia, and methanol. Building sovereign capability in these fuels could strengthen Australia’s energy security and strategic resilience by supporting a more secure fuel supply for critical maritime operations, including defence and government fleets.

As maritime fuel demand transitions over time, Australia has the potential to domestically produce a substantial share of the fuels it needs. The infrastructure, expertise and supply chains developed through maritime decarbonisation could therefore make a meaningful contribution to national energy resilience whilst creating new economic opportunities.

Like Australia, many other Asia-Pacific (APAC) countries are actively exploring pathways to diversify fuel supplies and establish new clean energy value chains. By supporting first-mover maritime decarbonisation initiatives like the Australia-East Asia iron ore green corridor, Australia can strengthen regional partnerships, contribute to shared APAC fuel security objectives, and position itself as a leading partner in the clean energy and green shipping corridors that will underpin future low-emission trade.

title: From Regulation to Implementation: Why the Flag State Matters
summary: As shipping navigates an increasingly complex regulatory landscape, the challenge is no longer simply adopting new rules, but ensuring that they work in practice. Decarbonisation, alternative fuels, d...
content:
As shipping navigates an increasingly complex regulatory landscape, the challenge is no longer simply adopting new rules, but ensuring that they work in practice. Decarbonisation, alternative fuels, digitalisation, safety and evolving seafarer requirements are placing new demands on shipowners, managers and crews, while also reshaping the role of Flag States.

In this context, The Bahamas Maritime Authority (BMA) is placing particular emphasis on practical implementation, early engagement with the industry and clear regulatory guidance. With a fleet of more than 1,800 vessels globally and a growing presence in Greece, the Authority is also positioning its Piraeus operation as an important link with one of the world’s leading shipping communities.

In an exclusive interview with Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide (www.hellenicshippingnews.com), Captain Dwain Hutchinson, CEO and MD at The Bahamas Maritime Authority, discusses the transition from policy to practice, the changes introduced under The Bahamas’ new Merchant Shipping Regulations, and the challenges facing shipping as the industry moves towards a lower-carbon, more technology-driven and increasingly skills-intensive future.

This year’s IMO theme for World Maritime Day is “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence”. Can you tell us what this actually means from a shipowners’ and managers’ perspective?

For owners and managers, it comes down to what happens once new requirements or standards are introduced following the adoption of international regulations. That is the point at which they must assess what those requirements mean for their vessels, their crews and their day-to-day operations.

This is where The Bahamas Maritime Authority, as a Flag State, has an important role to play. We must ensure that requirements are clearly communicated and supported by practical guidance to enable effective implementation. Equally important is the feedback we receive from owners, managers and seafarers, who are often the first to identify what works well in practice and where challenges may arise.

For me, that is the true meaning of “From Policy to Practice”. Agreeing and adopting regulations is only the first step. The real measure of success is whether those regulations achieve their intended objectives once they are embedded within management systems and applied on board ships.

Are we making ships and shipboard systems safer? Are we strengthening security? Are we improving environmental performance? Are we providing appropriate training and safeguarding the health and wellbeing of seafarers? Most importantly, are we giving those responsible for implementation a framework that is practical and workable? Those are the questions that define maritime excellence.

As regulation becomes more complex, how can Flag States help owners in understanding the changes? Is BMA actively involved in this process?

Owners are facing a rapidly evolving regulatory landscape. Decarbonisation, alternative fuels, digitalisation, and changes to safety and training requirements all bring new levels of complexity and practical implications for fleet operations.

One of the key responsibilities of a Flag State is to provide clarity, ensuring that stakeholders understand their obligations and can achieve compliance without unnecessary disruption to operations. The BMA is actively involved throughout the regulatory process.

Firstly, The Bahamas, through the BMA and in close consultation with shipowners and other industry partners, is actively represented at IMO meetings, contributing technical expertise while regulations are still being developed rather than waiting until they enter into force. This collaborative approach allows us to bring the practical experiences and concerns of owners, managers and seafarers directly into the regulatory discussion.

Secondly, once requirements have been adopted, we support implementation through Marine Notices, technical guidance, industry briefings and direct engagement with our clients. We want owners to understand what is coming well in advance, enabling them to prepare effectively rather than react at the last minute.

Finally, we continue to seek feedback on both the effectiveness of our guidance and the practical implementation of requirements. This engagement takes place directly with owners and managers, as well as through organisations such as the Bahamas Shipowners Association, ICS, CLIA, INTERTANKO and INTERCARGO.

What are the main changes undertaken so far in 2026 under the new suite of Merchant Shipping Regulations? What do these mean for owners?

The new regulations, which came into force on 1 April 2026, represent a significant modernisation of The Bahamas’ maritime legislative framework. The industry has evolved considerably, and it was important that our regulatory structure reflected the realities of modern shipping and contemporary administration.

The changes cover a broad range of areas, including registration, inspections, marine safety investigations and seafarer standards. We have also consolidated our fee structure and introduced updated provisions that support the use of digital records and electronic certification.

From an owner’s perspective, the key benefits are clarity, efficiency and flexibility. The revised framework makes requirements easier to understand and navigate, while providing a more adaptable foundation capable of responding to the pace of international regulatory change.

This was not change for its own sake. It was about ensuring that The Bahamas has a modern, resilient framework that supports today’s fleet while remaining adaptable to future developments.

The Bahamas’ role in this shifting environment is growing. Can you give us some data in terms of the fleet under the Flag and its presence both internationally and in Greece?

The Bahamas remains one of the world’s leading international ship registries, with more than 1,800 vessels representing approximately 72 million gross tonnes across a diverse range of ship types operating globally.

Greece is a particularly important market for us and has been for many years. As part of our commitment to providing localised service and closer engagement with clients, we established our Piraeus office in 2014.

Today, the Greek-owned fleet under the Bahamian flag comprises more than 275 vessels, representing approximately 13 million gross tonnes. This includes over 100 bulk carriers, as well as tankers, gas carriers, general cargo vessels, offshore vessels and yachts.

Beyond the statistics, Greece offers an unparalleled depth of maritime expertise and experience. Maintaining a permanent presence in Piraeus enables us to engage directly with owners and managers, providing support on registration, technical matters, seafarer documentation and a wide range of operational issues.

Which are the main issues and areas where you expect significant changes moving forward?

Decarbonisation will undoubtedly remain a dominant theme, but the focus must extend beyond emissions targets alone. The key questions are practical ones: how ships will achieve those targets, which fuels will be adopted, and how safety frameworks will evolve to support them.

The availability of trained personnel will be equally important. The transition to alternative fuels such as methanol, ammonia and hydrogen introduces new operational requirements and risks. Safe bunkering, handling and operation will require seafarers with specialised skills and training.

At the same time, advancing technologies are changing the skills profile required on board. Recruiting, developing and retaining the next generation of seafarers will therefore remain a major challenge. The human element also extends beyond competence to include health, welfare and wellbeing, all of which must remain central to the industry’s future.

title: DNV’s 2nd Energy Efficiency & Technologies Forum Puts Operational Evidence At The Centre Of Maritime Decarbonization
summary: Maritime decarbonization will depend on the industry’s ability to verify performance, understand economics and scale solutions based on operational experience, according to participants at DNV’s 2nd E...
content:
Maritime decarbonization will depend on the industry’s ability to verify performance, understand economics and scale solutions based on operational experience, according to participants at DNV’s 2nd Energy Efficiency & Technologies Forum in Athens.

The forum brought together shipowners, technology providers, academics and DNV experts to examine the practical readiness of energy-efficiency and decarbonization measures. Discussions focused on measured fuel savings, implementation challenges and the business case for hydrodynamic retrofits, wind-assisted propulsion, LNG and biomethane, shore power, emissions-data management, onboard carbon capture and nuclear propulsion.

Opening the forum, Jason Stefanatos, Global Decarbonization Director at DNV Maritime, emphasized the continued importance of energy efficiency in shipping’s transition:

“While alternative fuels will play a critical role in decarbonization, improving energy efficiency remains one of the most immediate and commercially attractive opportunities available to shipowners today. The challenge is to understand which solutions deliver measurable value under real operating conditions and how they can be implemented at scale.”

A recurring theme throughout the forum was the need to base investment decisions on measured operational performance rather than theoretical potential.

André Kauffeldt, Principal Engineer at DNV’s Ship Performance Center, presented findings from more than 180 bow-retrofit projects, while Katerina Prifti, HSQE Director/DPA/Vetting at Laskaridis Shipping, shared operational experience from the company’s evaluation of wind-assisted propulsion. The discussions highlighted how fuel savings and payback periods can vary significantly depending on vessel design, operating profile and trading pattern.

The economics of compliance also featured prominently. George Kriezis, Technical Director at Neptune Group of Companies, examined LNG and biomethane as part of long-term decarbonization strategies, highlighting the influence of fuel availability, lifecycle emissions and FuelEU Maritime compliance considerations on investment decisions and fleet economics.

Looking at other decarbonization measures, Lefteris Koukoulopoulos, Regional Decarbonization Specialist at DNV Maritime, discussed the readiness of shore power and the infrastructure challenges that continue to constrain wider adoption. While uptake is increasing in some vessel segments, access to shore-power connections remains limited in many ports.

Trusted and verified emissions data emerged as another key theme. Konstantinos Kordas, Performance Engineer at Navarone S.A., outlined the company’s fleet-level energy-efficiency strategy, while Vasileios Petousis of Seanergy Maritime Holdings, together with Mette Rønning Raabel and Lars Nyflot from DNV Maritime, highlighted the role of verified emissions data in supporting regulatory reporting, performance monitoring and operational decision-making.

The forum also explored technologies that remain at an earlier stage of adoption. Dimitris Koutsaftis, CCS Technical Product Manager at ERMA FIRST, and Chara Georgopoulou, Head of Maritime R&D and Advisory Greece at DNV Maritime, reviewed the opportunities and challenges associated with onboard carbon capture. Closing the event, Professor George Dimopoulos of the National Technical University of Athens examined the conditions under which nuclear propulsion could become relevant for selected shipping applications.

title: Strait of Hormuz security, decarbonisation among key issues discussed by BIMCO committees
summary: The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC)...
content:
The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC) and Marine Environment Committee (MEC) met on 30 September and 1 October.

Members considered the implications of regional conflicts, attacks on shipping, drones, mines and navigational disruption. The committees also discussed a broad range of other regulatory, safety and environmental issues affecting the day-to-day operation of ships.

These meetings are an important part of how we represent your interests. Our committees bring together industry expertise to identify practical challenges and help shape BIMCO’s positions in discussions with the IMO, governments and regulators.

Digitalisation was another major theme, including the opportunities it offers for efficiency, compliance and safety, as well as the growing importance of cyber security and supporting seafarers as technology develops.

Members also discussed the safe adoption of alternative fuels, including ammonia, hydrogen and methanol, and future safety frameworks for advanced modular nuclear reactors. The continued discussions on the IMO Net-Zero Framework and revisions to the EU ETS also received significant attention.

Operational and human factors featured prominently, including enclosed-space fatalities, hydrogen sulphide exposure, fatigue, crew welfare, criminalisation and suicide prevention.

On environmental regulation, members considered continuing challenges with ballast water management systems, including challenging water quality, reliability, spare parts and access to service engineers. The proposed legally-binding international convention on biofouling was also discussed, with an emphasis on ensuring that future requirements are practical, science-based and capable of consistent implementation across the global fleet.

Other topics included search and rescue and mixed migration, underwater radiated noise, marine plastics and plastic pellet transportation, and implementation of the Hong Kong Convention on ship recycling.

title: DNV Maritime Forecast to 2050: What The Latest Findings Mean For Greece And Cyprus?
summary: The maritime transition is moving forward, although the path ahead is still far from settled. Regulation continues to evolve, fuel markets are still taking shape, and yet many important decisions abou...
content:
The maritime transition is moving forward, although the path ahead is still far from settled. Regulation continues to evolve, fuel markets are still taking shape, and yet many important decisions about vessels, operations and investment need to be made today.

Lefteris Koukoulopoulos, Regional Decarbonization Specialist, Southeast Europe, DNV Maritime commented:

“This is why I find the 10th edition of DNV’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 particularly relevant. It looks at how shipping can plan across different regulatory and fuel-market outcomes, with new analysis on energy efficiency, low-GHG fuels and fleet strategy.

For me, one message stands out: energy efficiency is the most immediate and practical decarbonization solution available to shipowners today.

It offers shipowners a way to reduce fuel consumption and emissions today, while managing costs and keeping their options open for the future. Importantly, energy efficiency can create value regardless of which fuel pathway ultimately succeeds. The report shows that energy use across the global fleet could be reduced by up to 28% by 2050 through fleet renewal, operational improvements and retrofits.

This reflects many of the conversations I have been having in Greece and Cyprus. While most newbuilding orders, particularly in the tanker and bulk carrier segments, are still conventionally fuelled, shipowners are closely examining how they can integrate as many energy-efficient options as possible. It is a practical and flexible approach: improve performance today, while retaining the ability to respond as regulations, technologies and fuel markets evolve.

I see the Maritime Forecast as a useful starting point for these conversations. It does not offer one answer for every fleet. Instead, it helps us ask the right questions: where does it make sense to act now, which options should remain open, and how can today’s decisions remain robust as the market changes?

Shipping is undergoing an unprecedented technology and fuel transition to set the industry on a path towards net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. International and regional regulatory requirements are critical in determining the scale and pace of maritime decarbonization, driving shifts in uptake of fuels and technologies. Given the lifespan of newbuilds today, often beyond 2050, ships must be designed to meet future regulations, reducing risks and costs across fleets. This increases the importance of combining near-term actions, such as energy-efficiency improvements, with long-term flexibility to use low-GHG-emission fuels”.

The state of the transition

This report provides an update on the state of this transition, starting with the regulatory landscape. The delayed decision by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) targeting net-zero GHG emissions by or around 2050 is prolonging uncertainty. However, EU regulations and commercial pressures are already influencing investment decisions and operational choices.

Given uncertainty at the international level, we present four scenarios for possible future regulatory development. The key implication is not only that several regulatory pathways remain possible, but also that prolonged uncertainty at the IMO can increase the likelihood of additional regional regulations targeting international shipping.

Energy efficiency is becoming increasingly important: it reduces fuel use and emissions immediately, while also lowering the cost of operating on more expensive low-GHG fuels. For the world fleet, energy-efficiency measures and speed reductions can reduce energy use by up to 16% in 2030 compared to business-as-usual, and the potential towards 2050 is larger still. However, full maritime decarbonization will require a shift from fossil fuels to low-GHG fuels, complemented by other solutions such as onboard carbon capture and storage (OCCS) and potentially nuclear power.

title: DatamarLab to Release Executive Report on Maritime Shipping Emissions in Coming Weeks
summary: DatamarLab is preparing to release an Executive Report in the coming weeks that translates the results of its proof of concept on maritime shipping emissions into information to support decision-makin...
content:
DatamarLab is preparing to release an Executive Report in the coming weeks that translates the results of its proof of concept on maritime shipping emissions into information to support decision-making. Intended for shipowners, operators, ports, terminals, exporters and importers, the publication will show what analyzing a voyage can reveal about fuel choices, operational efficiency and the share of carbon emissions attributed to each shipment. DatamarLab’s Pioneer Sponsors will receive it first.

The release is one of the highlights of the third edition of DatamarLab’s newsletter, published in October 2026. Those interested in keeping up with upcoming releases and research progress can subscribe to the newsletter.

Subscribe to the DatamarLab newsletter to follow the Executive Report’s release, receive future editions and stay up to date on the initiative: https://www.datamar.com/pt/datamar-lab

What the Executive Report Covers

Organized into three parts—why measure, what was measured and what decisions this can inform—the report connects scientific findings with the issues facing companies involved in maritime trade.

In its analysis of fuels, the publication shows why alternatives with similar onboard emissions can yield different results when their full life cycles, including production, are considered. It also examines how engine technology and methane slip influence the climate performance of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

On operations, the report shows how emissions are distributed across the ten legs of the voyage studied and compares the contributions of activities at sea, at berth and at anchor. The vessel spent 17 days in port and 44 at sea. Simulations of the same voyage at 11, 16 and 23 knots allow an assessment of speed’s impact on emissions and the potential reductions associated with slower sailing.

The publication also analyzes the influence of variables such as draft, hull condition and engine efficiency at low loads, identifying the main sources of uncertainty in the estimates.

On allocating emissions among shipments, the report addresses the role of empty containers and shows how the choice of calculation basis—per TEU, metric ton or TEU-kilometer, with or without empty containers—changes carbon intensity indicators. This analysis helps explain why exporters using the same vessel and route may have different results.

Finally, the publication discusses the implications for contracts and commercial decisions: how a per-shipment emissions figure can help verify carbon surcharges and become part of freight quotes alongside rates and transit times.

Information for Different Supply Chain Participants

For shipowners and operators, the report offers an independent baseline of emissions per voyage that can help them assess and substantiate their figures. For ports and terminals, it provides a view of how time at berth and at anchor contributes to shipping’s carbon footprint.

For exporters, importers and freight forwarders, the aim is to show how to identify the share of emissions associated with each shipment, providing a basis for assessing charges and engaging with other parties involved in the operation.

A Single Voyage as a Starting Point

The report is based on the scientific paper from DatamarLab’s proof of concept, which has been completed and is scheduled for publication in October. The study models an actual voyage by the container ship M/V EVER FAME, covering 11 port calls and 13,913 nautical miles between the east coast of South America and Asia.

The analysis uses Datamar event data, including arrivals, berthings, departures, draft at each port call and cargo ownership at both ends. Ten fuel, engine and speed scenarios were evaluated, 982 exporters were identified and 3,251 shipment records were analyzed, each with its share of the voyage’s emissions.

The results are model estimates for one vessel on a single voyage, developed using engineering principles rather than onboard fuel consumption measurements. Work to extend the method to other vessels and routes is underway.

The work is part of the development of a collaborative decision-making framework for maritime shipping in South America. DatamarLab’s goal is to enable companies and regulators to work from a shared foundation of independent, scientifically grounded data, with an initial focus on decarbonization.

Follow Upcoming Releases

In addition to research progress, the DatamarLab newsletter features news and analysis on decarbonization and its implications for maritime shipping.

Subscribe to the DatamarLab newsletter

Companies interested in joining as Pioneer Sponsors, with early access to the report and a role in defining future topics and features, can contact datamarlab@datamar.com.br.

title: PATH TO NET ZERO: Shipping companies face slow low-carbon bunker transition
summary: Despite boasting improved carbon intensity, major shipping lines reported an alarming increase in their absolute greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, largely due to extended voyages. This uptick underscores a persistent reliance on cheap, high-carbon fuels, with 0.5%S fuel oil at $18.66/GJ remaining vastly more attractive than sustainable methanol at $48.69/GJ. Such a trajectory will inevitably challenge FuelEU Maritime compliance and expose operators to significant fines for failing to meet mandated bunker fuel intensity reductions.
content:
Major shipping companies have made progress in reducing the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of their operations but are struggling to achieve emission cuts in absolute terms.

In their latest annual reports, the world’s top 10 maritime companies by market capitalization — all of which have some degree of net-zero targets by 2050 or earlier — reported long-term declines in GHGs per transport work but rising emissions overall in 2025.

The development came as many ships were forced to take longer routes amid geopolitical conflicts and consumed more fuel, even as vessel operators were willing to invest in energy-efficiency measures that could yield healthy financial returns in a bullish oil market.

“With longer distances, the emissions per ton-mile goes down, but the total emissions of course go up,” Tore Longva, decarbonization director of classification society and maritime advisory DNV, told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. “A lot of the low-hanging energy efficiency measures are implemented … but a 25% further energy efficiency improvement is [still] possible towards 2050. Ultimately, however, low-GHG fuels will be needed to reach net-zero.”

Longva and all other industry experts interviewed for this article responded by email.

Green marine energy remains much more costly than conventional, oil-based fuels due to its limited availability. July’s average delivered bunker price for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil — the most popular marine fuel — was $18.66 per gigajoule in Singapore, compared with $20.05/GJ for LNG, $22.72/GJ for B24 bioblend, and $48.69/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts Global Bunker Cost Calculator.

Regulatory drivers

To reduce the price gap, the European Union has, since 2024, extended its emissions trading system to cover shipping and introduced the FuelEU Maritime rules in 2025 to cap GHG bunker fuel intensity.

The International Maritime Organization earlier approved the Net-Zero Framework, designed to place a cost on GHGs from ship operations globally from 2028. But its implementation is facing delays as fierce US opposition has prompted many of the UN agency’s member states to discuss revisions.

“IMO’s [Net-Zero Framework] is critical for what happens next,” said Tristan Smith, a professor at UCL Energy Institute in London. “Regional policy lacks the stringency to make a significant impact on shipping’s energy transition. … It is hard to see how it will enable any mass market participation in energy transition for the foreseeable future.”

Some in the shipping industry have echoed Smith’s view.

Wolfram Guntermann, director for regulatory affairs at German container line Hapag-Lloyd AG, one of the world’s largest listed shipping firms, said the IMO framework is highly important because shipping is a cross-border industry that requires globally aligned regulations.

“A common international fuel standard and emissions-pricing mechanism would provide greater investment certainty, support the scaling of low- and zero-emission fuels and reduce regulatory fragmentation,” Guntermann said.

Simon Bergulf, vice president for environment and climate at World Shipping Council, said the liner industry — represented by his organization — has invested $180 billion in ships capable of running on sustainable fuels such as bio-LNG and low-carbon methanol.

“[But] global regulations for a global industry are necessary to make it possible for carriers to operate on green fuels at scale, and to incentivize fuel and energy providers to invest in new production capacity,” Bergulf said.

Voluntary demand

Without sufficient global regulatory drivers, shipping companies have been seeking to provide sustainable freight services at higher prices in their pursuit of a financially viable energy transition. But demand on that front, often arising from cargo owners’ voluntary decarbonization efforts, has been falling.

A.P. Møller-Mærsk A/S reported that its biofuel and green methanol use nearly halved to 1,524 GWh in 2025, from 3,034 GWh in 2024, reversing an upward trend in recent years. The world’s largest listed shipping company cited lower voluntary demand as one of the reasons for the decline.

In the latest annual Shipping Decarbonization Survey by Boston Consulting Group, the organization found that cargo owners, on average, were willing to pay a 3% premium to transport goods on ships running on green fuels in 2025, down from 4.5% in 2024 and the lowest since 2022.

The share of cargo owners unwilling to pay any premiums increased by 4 percentage points in 2025, while those inclined to pay premiums of over 20% fell to zero from 3% in the prior year, according to the survey of 125 logistics executives.

“Cost management has moved to the top of the agenda, while other priorities include energy security and resilience,” Boston Consulting Group said. “Low-carbon shipping is increasingly deprioritized.”

Outlook for shipping sector

Although long-term deep decarbonization requires large amounts of green fuels at affordable prices, major Japanese shipping firms Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha and Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd. said they could achieve substantial GHG cuts through improved energy efficiency and use of currently available alternative fuels — such as LNG and biofuels — for the interim period.

“We believe meaningful emissions reductions remain achievable through measures within our direct control, including energy-efficiency improvements, fleet modernization, retrofits and operational optimization,” NYK told Platts in an email.

MOL said the company’s goal is to reduce emissions without relying “excessively” on uncertain regulatory developments or technological breakthroughs.

“We are currently advancing decarbonization primarily through the use of LNG, while working toward a future transition to zero-emission fuels such as ammonia,” the company said.

Fotios Katsoulas, research director for alternative fuels at S&P Global Energy Horizons, said shipping companies are likely to focus more on decarbonization means at hand if regulators continue to have difficulties implementing GHG rules.

title: Konecranes sets new long-term climate ambition that supports its customer industries’ decarbonization efforts
summary: Konecranes, a supplier, announced a 90% GHG emission reduction target by 2050, framing "low-emission solutions" as a "great business opportunity." This distant ambition does little to address the immediate carbon intensity of vessels or their continued reliance on heavy fuel oil. Shipping needs verifiable, immediate reductions to avoid FuelEU Maritime fines and improve dismal CII ratings, not just long-term supplier promises.
content:
Konecranes commits to a long-term climate ambition to complement its recently upgraded near-term science-based targets. The company aims to reduce its absolute Scope 1, 2 and 3 greenhouse gas emissions 90% by 2050 from base year 2019.

The new long-term ambition builds on the company’s current near-term climate targets to reduce absolute greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 60% from Scope 1 & 2 and 50% from Scope 3 including purchased goods and services and use of sold products by 2030 compared to a base year 2019, validated by Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), as well as its carbon-neutral manufacturing* target.

The new long-term target reflects the same absolute GHG emissions reduction ambition as defined by the SBTi Net-Zero Standard and aligns with the pathway to limit global warming to 1.5C under the Paris Agreement.

“We reached our original 2030 target of halving Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions already in 2022. Last year, we raised the target level for 2030 and focus now on achieving it. This year we reached another milestone by completing the electrification of all product lines. Our electric equipment offering helps customers reduce emissions from their own operations while supporting our company’s future value chain emission reduction potential. Today’s announcement builds on our efforts and long-term commitment towards climate action. We see providing low-emission solutions as a great business opportunity, while supporting our customer industries in their decarbonization efforts,” says Marko Tulokas, President & CEO, Konecranes.

To reach the 2050 ambition, Konecranes will continue reducing emissions across its operations and value chain. The company’s biggest contribution is to provide customers with low-emission solutions, such as electric equipment. Additionally, Konecranes advances the use of lower-emission materials and circular solutions across its offering and continues to decarbonize its own operations. Achieving the ambition will also require broader market transformation like the decarbonization of customer industries, lower-emission steel production and transportation, and cleaner energy systems.

Konecranes believes that the most effective contribution to climate change mitigation is achieved through reducing absolute GHG emissions. Previously, Konecranes had committed to setting a SBTi-validated long-term net-zero target. After the recent launch of the SBTi Net-Zero Standard 2.0, with increased emphasis on neutralization of residual emissions and uncertainty around the future implementation and development of the standard, Konecranes decided not to pursue SBTi validation of its long-term climate target. The company’s long-term climate ambition is aligned with the standard’s requirements on absolute GHG emission reductions but does not include neutralization of residual emissions.

Konecranes’ science-based near-term targets, upgraded and revalidated by SBTi in 2025, remain unchanged. For further details about Konecranes climate targets and the transition plan, please click here.

To learn about the Konecranes sustainability agenda, actions and progress, please see the Sustainability Statement 2025Opens in new tab and Konecranes.com/sustainability.

title: New insight brief explores why maritime decarbonisation matters for Australia
summary: Australia's new brief, 'Why maritime decarbonisation matters', offers a high-level discussion on economic opportunities without detailing specific plans to reduce its ships' substantial carbon intensity. The document remains silent on the immediate impact of FuelEU Maritime fines on Australian trade, nor does it specify timelines for phasing out heavy fuel oil (HFO) usage. Such vague explorations risk delaying tangible emission reductions, leaving Australia's fleet to continue operating with excessive carbon footprints and poor CII ratings.
content:
With around 99% of Australia’s trade by volume carried by sea, the global transition to lower-emission shipping could have significant implications for the country’s economy.

This insight brief, 'Why maritime decarbonisation matters for Australia', explores how Australia can position itself to capture the economic opportunities emerging from maritime decarbonisation, from strengthening export competitiveness and industrial capability to improving energy security, productivity and economic resilience.

While delayed action could limit Australia’s ability to shape emerging markets and secure long-term value from the shipping transition, early engagement could help the country strengthen its position in the global maritime economy.

The brief examines the challenges and opportunities for Australia as shipping moves towards lower-emission fuels and technologies, and considers how maritime decarbonisation can support the country’s broader economic interests.

title: People are the powerbase of the shipping business
summary: Despite Asia's growing maritime influence and significant investment in "decarbonisation" technologies, this report offers no concrete data on actual carbon intensity reductions or decreased HFO consumption. Highlighting innovation without disclosing real-world fleet emissions or progress against FuelEU Maritime targets risks being pure greenwashing. Until tangible proof of lowered operational emissions and adherence to CII ratings is provided, the industry's environmental commitment remains questionable.
content:
Decarbonisation, digitalisation, shifting patterns of global trade and an increasing level of influence from Asia are continuing to reshape the shipping, logistics and trading sectors. With this year’s WISTA International AGM and Conference taking place in Kuala Lumpur, the association’s president, Elpi Petraki, explains why there are important lessons to learn from the region as the challenges facing the industry demand more than new technologies and innovation.

Asia’s changing maritime landscape

As the world’s largest maritime market, Asia offers an extraordinary degree of maritime capabilities and specialities. It is home to the world’s leading shipbuilding nations, some of its largest ports, many major shipowners and a multitude of maritime service providers. Its financial centres are globally significant, while regional governments are powerhouse investors in decarbonisation, digitalisation and emerging technologies.

According to Clarkson’s Research and United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD), China, the Republic of Korea and Japan accounted for 91% of ships completed globally in 2025. Meanwhile, Singapore retained its position as the world’s leading maritime centre for the 13th year running in the 2026 Xinhua-Baltic International Shipping Centre Development Index (ISCDI). And the Philippines remains the world’s largest supplier of STCW-certified seafarers, with approximately 460,147 active Filipino seafarers according to the 2026 BIMCO and International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) Seafarer Workforce Report.

As such, Asia’s influence on international shipping is growing. Across the region, new technologies and operating models are being developed, tested and deployed, with innovation seen in digital twins, AI and autonomous vessels, and in alternative fuels and smart-port infrastructure.

China, Japan, South Korea, and hubs such as Singapore, are also providing real-world environments for developers to move from concept to reality. While Hong Kong, Malaysia and other maritime centres contribute critical expertise across finance, professional services, ports and logistics.

But the scale of maritime operations and willingness to invest in new technology offer only part of the explanation for Asia’s success. Across the region, governments, industry and educational institutions are also coming together to form highly integrated clusters that invest not only in technology and infrastructure, but also in people.

This year’s Maritime Singapore Master Plan, for example, identifies the development of a future-ready maritime workforce as one of four key strategies through which it will continue its long-running success story. Several other government programmes are running to support new career pathways, upskilling and leadership development whose content includes modules specifically designed to encourage people to consider and nurture a career in the industry.

Regionally, the maritime focus is far from unique. In India, targeted initiatives such as the government’s Saga Mein Samman programme aims to create a gender equitable workforce, improve women’s welfare and significantly increase their participation in the sector, as it looks to achieve a 12% increase in the number of women employed in technical maritime roles by 2030. Similarly, the IMO-Republic of Korea SMART-C Women’s Project, provides specialised training and leadership skills development for women in fields related to digitalisation and decarbonisation.

In a region encouraged by sustained growth across the maritime space, these investments and collaborations are opportunities to attract new and more diverse talents to industry. They demonstrate a clear understanding that a maturing industry cannot prepare for the future without investing in the renewal and revitalisation of its workforce.

People are at the heart of the industry’s transformation, and success will be reliant on recognising this and securing access to the widest possible talent pool. Because maritime’s greatest asset has always been its people, and research consistently shows that diverse teams are more effective.

From advocacy to action

However, as I have said many times during my tenure as WISTA International President, inclusion is not about replacing men with women. Rather, it is about working together to empower everyone and acknowledging that women have the skills and experience to lead effectively, make decisions and address the challenges facing the industry.

Over recent years, the conversation around diversity and inclusion in maritime has changed. There is greater awareness of the challenges women face, better data on representation and growing recognition of the link between inclusive leadership, a future ready workforce and a strong, resilient industry.

WISTA International has played a key role in changing the narrative surrounding gender equity and equality in maritime and has worked closely with its partners to enhance research, professional development, leadership and collaboration across the sector. The 2024 IMO-WISTA Women in Maritime Survey has provided important benchmarks for monitoring progress, and the IMO-WISTA-WMU Gender Inclusive Leadership and Empowerment Training Course, for example, addresses the need for a stronger, more sustainable leadership pipeline.

There have also been encouraging signs that the industry is moving from simply understanding the importance of inclusion to embedding it within policy and professional standards.

The 2024 Women in Maritime survey indicated a modest increase in the number of women in C-suite positions in multiple sectors and found that companies with women in leadership positions were also more likely to have policies in place that enhance diversity and inclusion.

Elsewhere, few can be unaware of the 2017 and 2021 surveys conducted by WISTA International, Anglo Eastern, the International Seafarers Welfare and Assistance Network and the International Chamber of Shipping, and the shocking levels of bullying, harassment and sexual assault women working on ships experience. Accordingly, STCW Code amendments which – from 1 January 2026 – made training to prevent and respond to violence and harassment mandatory for all seafarers are wholly welcome.

This represents an important shift. Now, creating a safe and respectful workplace is no longer simply a matter of individual commitment or corporate policy; it is recognised as part of the professional standards required for those working at sea.

But awareness alone is not enough. The challenge that remains is how to turn recognition into lasting change and create the conditions in which women and other under-represented groups can join and succeed in a maritime career. That means continuing to challenge assumptions, investing in skills and leadership development, and making inclusion integral in how organisations operate rather than something to be discussed separately.

Greater visibility and representation are important, but we must be careful not to confuse visibility with equality, or progress with completion.

The next chapter

The upcoming WISTA International AGM and Conference in Kuala Lumpur comes at an key moment for the shipping, logistics and trading sectors. Co-hosted by WISTA Hong Kong SAR China, WISTA Malaysia and WISTA Singapore, the conference reflects WISTA’s long-standing commitment to collaboration and will bring together perspectives from across the region to advance conversations around sustainability, technology and inclusive leadership.

The maritime industry is changing. We have more data, greater awareness and a better understanding of the important role diversity and inclusion play in shaping the future of the industry.

The global maritime industry can also learn a lot from Asia, where long-term investment, structured approaches and coherent responses to opportunities have played a profound role in shifting the centre of global economics.

But for WISTA, it has never been about just one president, one conference, or even one initiative. It has always been about working together to enhance diversity and inclusion, and to create an industry that empowers and respects everyone.

title: Financing a More Resilient and Sustainable Energy System for Shipping
summary: Despite grand commitments, the shipping industry's transition to zero-emission fuels remains largely stalled, with critical projects stuck due to an 'inadequate willingness to pay' for cleaner alternatives. The failure to adequately price carbon externalities keeps HFO and other fossil fuels artificially cheap, directly undermining demand for green methanol and ammonia, which are 2 to 6 times more expensive on an energy-equivalent basis. This inaction ensures continued reliance on high-carbon fuels, guaranteeing excessive emissions and future FuelEU Maritime fines for operators prioritizing short-term savings over genuine decarbonization.
content:
Image Source: Pexels

This is part of the essay series: Sagarmanthan Edit 2026.

The maritime sector’s energy system is among the most fossil fuel-dependent and a significant contributor to emissions. This exposes the industry to supply chokepoints, volatile fuel prices, regulatory uncertainty, stranded assets and more. Diversifying the energy base is, therefore, an investment in resilience. It is also an opportunity; unlike the old energy system, whose geography is fixed by geology, the new one will be shaped by renewable power potential and industrial ambition – a space many countries, like India, are well placed to contest.

Shipping has committed to becoming more resilient and sustainable. This commitment remains largely intact despite a longer-than-expected Net Zero Framework (NZF) process and a more difficult climate transition environment. However, implementation has been slow and is slowing down, especially in Zero and Near Zero emission solutions (ZNZ). Critical fuel projects are stuck at pre-Final Investment Decision (FID), and enabling infrastructure such as bunkering, pipelines and storage is not yet built. The transition raises hard questions – for instance, what ships to buy and when, where to produce new fuels, and how energy trade and the bunkering network could change. Many are difficult to solve while there is a cost gap between incumbent and ZNZ fuels.

Pricing the Carbon Externality

The binding constraint is inadequate willingness to pay. This materialises as a lack of demand commitment, making many ZNZ projects near impossible to finance – the well-discussed offtake bottleneck. ZNZ fuels cannot compete on price; at historical price levels, green methanol has cost two to five times conventional bunker fuel on an energy-equivalent basis, and green ammonia at least two to six times. This is chiefly because the externality of consuming carbon is not accounted for – fossil fuels are too cheap, underpriced by at least US$6.7tn per year based on 2024 IMF estimates. The world already pays for historical carbon consumption through loss of life and economic costs from heatwaves, floods and other climate events – these will only grow. The task is to ensure these costs are reflected in the price we pay for fossil fuels, not deferred.

ZNZ fuels cannot compete on price; at historical price levels, green methanol has cost two to five times conventional bunker fuel on an energy-equivalent basis, and green ammonia at least two to six times.

Shipping recognised this and created the NZF, which currently proposes a global price on emissions. However, the NZF has not yet been adopted; it is unlikely to take effect before 2029, and the carbon price it would ultimately set is not yet settled.

Measures for the Medium and Short Run

While efforts to implement optimal global policy continue, other measures can drive change. Sub-global policy could price the externality sooner and hedge against further delay or a global carbon price lower than needed to close the gap. Research and innovation are the main route to fundamentally cut the cost of production for ZNZ fuels. Both are essential, but neither delivers quickly.
