Building new strategic infrastructure can progress in parallel and will lay the foundations for a scale-up. The lead times for fuel plants, storage and bunkering, and other infrastructure can be 2–5 years. First-of-a-kind risks raise financing, construction and other costs until they are dispelled. Other sectors offer cautionary tales on the pitfalls of not doing so – evidenced by the 5–15-year connection queues delaying the renewable power rollout in many countries, creating huge costs and missed opportunity.

Routes2FID

Despite the challenging environment, there is still sufficient push – for instance, from India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission, EU ETS, and FuelEU Maritime – to build viable business cases in select projects. India offers some of the best examples, for instance, SECI’s recent contracts for green ammonia at US$572–744 per tonne – among the lowest observed. This is unsurprising. India pairs an advantageous renewable energy endowment with supportive industrial policy – the IEA counts India as one of the few places where tenders have converted into final investment decisions (FIDs). Future energy corridors may also look different, giving India an opportunity to establish export lanes. These lighthouse cases demonstrate sustainable paths to scale, kickstart learning-by-doing efficiencies, and create the market; identifying and supporting them is vital.

India pairs an advantageous renewable energy endowment with supportive industrial policy – the IEA counts India as one of the few places where tenders have converted into final investment decisions (FIDs). Future energy corridors may also look different, giving India an opportunity to establish export lanes.

A lot of support has already been committed to the sector (over US$40 billion additional into hydrogen in the last year alone), but conversion remains limited (hydrogen FIDs fell again in 2025). There may be scope to deploy support more efficiently and crowd in private capital. Enhanced coordination between concessional capital, commercial capital and policy, deployed in a targeted way, could help strategic projects on the edge of FID. The renewable power scale-up offers examples. In European offshore wind, public levers such as contracts for difference, concessional lending targeted at market failures and deliberate policy, for instance, socialising site assessment and grid connection costs, were able to reduce and share risks. This helped to make the sector financeable for private investors such as pension funds, infrastructure investors, and project lenders. The UK’s Green Investment Bank, for instance, attracted around US$2.50 for every US$1 of public funds invested.

Coordination of this kind is difficult. Each party arrives with different priorities, understandings and capabilities. Resolving it requires: (i) establishing a common quantitative language of project returns, such as a broader levelised cost of production metric, (ii) considering a range of finance and policy instruments including innovative mechanisms and best practice from elsewhere, (iii) analysing different scenarios for capital efficiency and burden sharing, and (iv) quantifying the impact of support levers and packages on the competitiveness and holistic returns of ZNZ projects.

Shipping’s transition finance environment has entered a period of great uncertainty. Bankability of decarbonisation projects will not materialise at scale without significant carbon pricing, and effort toward this end remains essential.

These can facilitate action-oriented discussions in small but complete groups of stakeholders who want to support a given strategic project. Such a group is most effective when curated to remain nimble: able to discuss commercially sensitive information, yet complete so all types of levers can be explored and stacked. In this setup, stakeholders could quantify the impact of existing levers and analyse the remaining gap to FID, surface overlooked levers and what it might take for members to commit to them, identify missing stakeholders to crowd in, and more. This is the approach of our Routes2FID project. As a non-profit in maritime decarbonisation, we are committed to supporting the industry in the energy transition and open to connecting with any organisation that may benefit from a discussion.

Shipping’s transition finance environment has entered a period of great uncertainty. Bankability of decarbonisation projects will not materialise at scale without significant carbon pricing, and effort toward this end remains essential. In parallel, continued support for the pipeline of critical infrastructure and the groundwork for scale would prepare the sector to respond when demand signals firm up. AM Green’s AMGA-K1 green ammonia plant in Kakinada reached FID in 2024 and is one of the largest under construction worldwide. Four ammonia dual-fuel vessels ordered in H1 2026 will be built in an Indian shipyard. India has built a strong environment for ZNZ fuels and could be a key enabler of a more resilient energy system for shipping and beyond. Closing the gap on projects like these is where this effort begins.

Lee Joh Hann leads transition finance and systems modelling work at the Lloyd’s Register Maritime Decarbonisation Hub.

title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
summary: An IMO study projects hybrid-electric ferries could cut Sea of Marmara GHG emissions by 63% and save €492 million in damages. Yet, this remains a theoretical "optimum scenario" with significant investment and infrastructure hurdles, not a funded commitment. Meanwhile, the region's 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries continue their business-as-usual operations, likely burning high-carbon fuels and exceeding CII targets.
content:
Türkiye’s Sea of Marmara ferry network could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by switching to a mix of hybrid and fully electric vessels, while avoiding nearly half a billion euros in health and environmental damage costs and supporting around 1,100 jobs a year, according to a new IMO study.

Commissioned by IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 programme in partnership with Türkiye’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure, the study assessed 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries carrying vehicles and passengers across 26 ports. The network transports around 25 million passengers and seven million vehicles each year.

Significant potential to cut emissions

The study found that battery-electric and hybrid propulsion are technically feasible options across all Ro-Pax and Ro-Ro ferry operations assessed in the Sea of Marmara.

It identified an optimum scenario combining hybrid and fully electric vessels to balance emissions reductions and costs. Under this scenario, annual GHG emissions could fall by around 63% by 2050 compared with business-as-usual operations using diesel fuel.

The transition would also reduce local air pollution and could avoid an estimated €492 million in cumulative health and environmental damage costs.

Going further, converting the entire fleet to fully electric operations could cut GHG emissions by 84% by 2050. This could rise to as much as 95% if Türkiye’s electricity grid decarbonizes in line with its 2053 net-zero target.

The study identified no major technical barriers to electrification. The main challenges to large-scale deployment are charging infrastructure, upfront investment, coordinated energy planning and the domestic regulatory framework.

Building on Türkiye’s shipbuilding strength

Ferry electrification would build on Türkiye established shipbuilding expertise, boosting clean technology industries in the country and reducing reliance on imported marine fuels.

Under the optimum hybrid-electric scenario, the required investment could support an average of around 1,100 jobs a year through to 2050. Vessel construction and retrofit jobs are expected to be concentrated in Turkish shipyards.

Moving towards implementation

To turn these findings into action, the study recommends a coordinated approach involving government, municipalities, ports, ferry operators and the energy sector.

Priority actions include:

expanding shoreside charging infrastructure and high-voltage grid connections at ports, supported by long-term port concessions that include charging infrastructure;

securing a low-carbon electricity supply at ports, including by allowing ports to generate, use and sell locally produced low-carbon electricity;

introducing targeted financial incentives, mobilizing blended finance, and using emissions-based port fees to encourage cleaner vessels;

integrating electrification into transport and energy planning;

embedding environmental criteria into public ferry procurement; and

supporting detailed feasibility studies and pilot projects that can demonstrate commercial viability before wider deployment.

GreenVoyage2050 and Türkiye’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure are now looking to advance a first pilot electrification project in the Sea of Marmara to demonstrate the technical, environmental and commercial benefits identified in the study.

Download the full study

About GreenVoyage2050

The GreenVoyage2050 Programme supports developing countries in reducing greenhouse gas emissions from shipping, in line with the IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships. Through technical assistance, capacity building, policy support and pilot projects, the programme helps countries identify practical pathways towards maritime decarbonization while fostering innovation, investment and international collaboration.

title: GTT Marine and Normec Verifavia strengthen partnership to simplify maritime emissions compliance
summary: GTT Marine and Normec Verifavia announced an integration to automate emissions data exchange, ostensibly simplifying compliance under schemes like FuelEU Maritime. This tool aims to streamline reporting and verification processes, yet offers no guarantee of tangible reductions in carbon intensity or egregious HFO consumption. Improved data consistency is welcome, but dirtiestships.com demands operational shifts to avoid FuelEU fines and ensure vessels actually meet or exceed their CII ratings, not just report them efficiently.
content:
GTT Marine, a business unit of the GTT Group, and Normec Verifavia, announce a new integration between GTT Marine’s Vesper Insights solution and the Normec Verifavia Emissions Verification dashboard, enabling automated data exchange and continuous emissions verification for shipping operators.

The integration enables the secure and automated transfer of vessel performance, voyage and emissions data directly into Normec Verifavia’s verification dashboard. By eliminating manual file exchanges and reducing data handling across multiple systems, ship operators can streamline compliance processes while improving data consistency and transparency throughout the reporting cycle.

Combined with data from across GTT Marine’s digital ecosystem, the integration supports a continuous approach to emissions verification. Rather than relying on periodic submissions and year-end reconciliation exercises, operators gain ongoing visibility into the quality and status of their compliance data throughout the reporting year.

The solution is designed to address the growing complexity of maritime emissions reporting. It supports a wide range of fuel pathways, including Bio-LNG and other low-carbon fuels, while supporting operators manage compliance obligations under EU ETS, FuelEU Maritime, EU and UK MRV, IMO DCS and CII requirements. By combining automated data exchange, continuous verification and advanced compliance monitoring, the integration reduces administrative workload, enables earlier identification of potential issues and provides greater confidence in regulatory reporting.

Building on their collaboration, this latest development marks the transition to a direct, standardised data pipeline between the two platforms and reinforces their shared commitment to simplifying emissions compliance through trusted data and digitalisation. The integrated approach is already supporting multiple mutual customers across different fleet segments.

“As emissions reporting requirements continue to evolve, ship-owners need greater visibility, accuracy and efficiency across the compliance process,” said Rajat Bishnoi, Business Unit Director, Shipping Emissions & Performance, Normec Verifavia. “By integrating directly with GTT Marine’s digital ecosystem, we can provide continuous verification supported by high-quality operational data, enabling customers to identify potential issues earlier and manage their compliance obligations more effectively.”

title: Opsealog whitepaper identifies the “missing loop” behind offshore fleets’ data problem
summary: Opsealog's whitepaper exposes a critical 'missing loop' in offshore fleets, where abundant data fails to translate into actionable decisions for fuel efficiency. Despite investments in digital tools, many vessels continue to burn excessive fuel, risking higher carbon intensity ratings and future FuelEU Maritime fines due to a lack of accountability and interpretation. While the MV Flat Confidence demonstrated 1,984 tonnes of CO2 savings through structured monitoring, the industry's widespread "conversion gap" means thousands of tonnes of preventable emissions are still being released.
content:
Opsealog, a provider of data integration and performance management services for the marine offshore industry, today published a new whitepaper arguing that the offshore industry’s data problem is conversion rather than collection. The Conversion Gap: What Offshore Fleets Lose Between Data and Decision draws on a decade of work across more than 1,000 offshore support vessels to explain why fleets that have invested heavily in digital tools still struggle to turn that data into faster, better decisions.

The paper’s central finding is what Opsealog calls the “missing loop.” Most digital tools are deployed on the assumption that data will convert itself into operational decisions. In practice, conversion requires someone accountable for reading the data, someone qualified to interpret it, and a mechanism for decision-making and implementation that sees action taken back on the vessel. When any one of those three elements is missing, OSV operators end up with dashboards nobody owns, reports that never travel back to the people who filed them, and limited meaningful action to improve vessel performance.

“Nobody gets fitter simply by wearing a smartwatch. Progress begins when data is turned into recommendations, and recommendations into action. Offshore fleets are no different, they need to turn data into actionable insights,” said Guillaume Robert, Chief Product & Technology Officer at Opsealog.

The paper backs this up with results from Opsealog’s own work. On the ‘MV Flat Confidence’, a Ghanaian-owned AHTS (Anchor Handling Tug Supply) operating under a long-term Tullow Ghana contract, a year of structured fuel monitoring saved 732.6 m³ of fuel and 1,984 tonnes of CO2, worth close to $850,000 at current fuel prices.

Applied across a 24-vessel mixed fleet off Angola over six months, the same method saved 1,108 m³ of fuel and 3,055 tonnes of CO2, worth roughly $1.85 million.

A third case study shows what happens when the data is right, but the decision stalls: a vessel caught between conflicting instructions from its charterer and shipowner, resolved only once both parties sat down and reviewed the same figures together.

The timing matters too, with EU MRV already covering offshore vessels of 400 GT and above, and the European Commission’s July 2026 proposals potentially extending the EU ETS to smaller offshore vessels from 2031. Norway has gone further, confirming greenhouse gas intensity cuts for vessels operating on its continental shelf from 2029. Rystad Energy estimates most of the current fleet, including LNG dual-fuel vessels, would miss the first threshold as things stand today. For operators, the paper argues, the fastest lever available is to run the existing fleet on data it can already defend, instead of waiting for new vessels or fuels.

“We’ve spent a decade proving that offshore fleets can collect more data than ever. The real test now is whether that data changes what happens on deck. This paper is about closing the loop between insight and action, vessel by vessel,” said Arnaud Dianoux, Founder & CEO of Opsealog.

The whitepaper also includes detailed breakdowns of where offshore digital programmes most commonly break down, and a short self-assessment allowing fleet operators to score where their own operation sits between collecting data and converting it into results, and identify which archetype reflects their current approach; the Collector, the Firefighter and the Converter.

Source: Opsealog

title: Brazil’s IMO proposal for ISWG-GHG 22: how compliance, surplus trading, and the facility could work
summary: Brazil's IMO proposal for ISWG-GHG 22 introduces a "flexible compliance system" that risks weakening the Net-Zero Framework's ambition by adjusting initial stringency and allowing transferable surplus units. This mechanism could enable vessels to purchase "compliance units" instead of achieving genuine carbon intensity reductions through operational changes or cleaner fuels. Such trading schemes, mirroring early FuelEU Maritime challenges, often provide avenues for continued high-carbon fuel usage without robust accountability.
content:
The negotiations around the IMO Net-Zero Framework have moved into an interesting phase. Following the decision not to adopt the draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI in October 2025, IMO Member States have spent much of 2026 considering how the framework could be adjusted without reopening the entire package negotiated at MEPC 83. Brazil’s contribution ISWG-GHG 22/2/12, submitted ahead of the September 2026 intersessional working group meeting (ISWG-GHG 22), is particularly relevant in this context because it attempts to address several of the concerns that have prevented agreement while preserving most of the underlying compliance architecture.

The IMO ISWG-GHG 22 Brazil proposal’s starting point is relatively conservative. Its stated preference remains adoption of the IMO Net-Zero Framework as negotiated, with changes only where they are considered necessary to achieve agreement. The alternatives contained in its submission are therefore presented as compromise options. The global GHG Fuel Intensity standard would remain, as would ship-level compliance balances, Surplus Units, Remedial Units and financial support for zero- and near-zero fuels. Changes concern the initial stringency of the targets, the presentation of the economic element, and the institutional structure through which compliance contributions would be collected and redistributed.

Similar to the initial proposal, Brazil wants the framework to operate explicitly as a flexible compliance system. A ship that reaches the required GHG intensity through its own fuels or technologies would comply directly and would not make a compliance payment. A ship that performs even better could create transferable surplus. Only where physical performance is insufficient would the company need to balance the remaining deficit through compliance units.

At the same time, the first year of FuelEU Maritime gives the industry a useful real-world example of how such flexibility can develop once a compliance market becomes operational. FuelEU has shown that surplus markets can facilitate compliance very effectively, but it has also exposed a more complicated question: the cheapest way of producing compliance is not necessarily the fuel pathway that policymakers ultimately may want to see scale in the long term. The current European experience therefore provides a useful lens through which to assess both the strengths and the remaining weaknesses of the Brazilian proposal.

The framework would remain built around GHG Intensity

The basic technical architecture remains unchanged. Ships would be measured against an annual GHG Intensity calculated on a well-to-wake basis and expressed in gCO₂eq/MJ. The draft framework uses a reference value of 93.3 gCO₂eq/MJ, representing the average GHG intensity of international shipping in 2008, and annual targets are expressed as percentage reductions against this reference value (just as in the original IMO NZF proposal).

An important feature of the IMO framework is that it contains two separate GFI thresholds. The Base Target establishes the less stringent minimum trajectory, while the Direct Compliance Target requires a significantly deeper reduction. The position of a vessel relative to these two thresholds determines whether it generates surplus, incurs a Tier 1 deficit or incurs both Tier 1 and Tier 2 deficits. This two-level design is central to the economic architecture because it prevents the market for transferable surplus from becoming the only mechanism through which the regulatory signal is transmitted.

Brazil proposes retaining this structure but making the choices available to shipping companies more explicit in the legal text. Its proposed wording for Regulation 32 would state that a ship can comply either directly through fuels, technologies or energy sources, or by balancing its compliance deficit through the cancellation of banked or traded surplus units and Remedial Units (RU) obtained through contributions to the IMO mechanism. Draft Regulation 36 would similarly clarify that each ship may voluntarily choose between direct compliance and balancing its deficit.

While nuanced, this is politically important because Brazil also proposes removing references to “GHG emissions pricing”. Its argument is that the system should not be understood as imposing a general levy on every tonne of shipping emissions. Instead, the economic element provides an alternative compliance route where direct physical compliance is unavailable or commercially unattractive. A company would therefore compare the cost of changing its fuel or technology with the cost of acquiring the units necessary to balance the resulting deficit.

A softer introduction, followed by a more demanding trajectory

Brazil also proposes a slower initial reduction trajectory. The submission shifts the implementation dates by one year following the delay in adoption and defers several of the originally negotiated reduction levels. Brazil explains that the adjustment is intended to respond to concerns about the availability of compliant fuels, the maturity of supply chains and the economic impact of introducing the mechanism too quickly.

The unusual feature is the treatment of the first two years. In 2029 and 2030, the Base Target and Direct Compliance Target would be identical. Brazil explicitly proposes this transitional arrangement to reduce the volume of revenue collected during the early implementation period and to give IMO additional time to establish the institutional systems required for larger-scale collection and redistribution. From 2031 onward, however, the two targets separate sharply and the full two-tier architecture becomes relevant.

Brazil does not propose reducing the long-term ambition indefinitely. At the other end of the trajectory, the submission would replace the previously envisaged 65% Base Target reduction in 2040 with a 70% reduction in 2041.

Surplus units would turn over-compliance into a tradable asset

A ship whose GFI is lower than the Direct Compliance Target would generate a positive compliance balance and become eligible for surplus units. The units correspond to the positive balance in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent. They can subsequently be transferred to another ship, banked for future use or voluntarily cancelled as a mitigation contribution.

This creates a genuine global compliance market somewhat similar to the already known FuelEU Maritime. Vessels with access to low-GHG fuels or technologies could generate compliance beyond their own requirements and sell that value to vessels facing higher physical decarbonisation costs. The economic effect is similar in principle to FuelEU Maritime: reductions take place where they are cheapest, while ships with fewer available options can remain compliant through the market rather than being forced into an immediate fuel switch.

There is nevertheless an important distinction between simply meeting the Base Target and becoming a supplier of surplus. Under the IMO architecture, the positive balance is calculated against the more stringent Direct Compliance Target. A vessel can therefore satisfy the Base Target and still generate no surplus units at all. Once the two targets separate from 2031, the threshold for becoming a surplus generator becomes materially more demanding than the minimum GFI trajectory.

That structure means that not every marginal improvement in vessel GFI automatically creates tradable supply. If the Direct Compliance Target requires a 19% reduction while the Base Target requires only 6%, as proposed for 2031, a vessel operating somewhere between those levels remains compliant with the Base Target but has not reached direct compliance. The resulting difference is dealt with through the Tier 1 mechanism rather than being ignored.

Tier 1 and Tier 2 are the key to understanding the economic mechanism

The distinction between Tier 1 and Tier 2 is one of the most important elements of the draft framework as well as the Brazilian proposal and can easily be overlooked. A vessel operating above the Direct Compliance Target but still below the Base Target has a Tier 1 compliance deficit. If its GFI also exceeds the Base Target, the additional emissions above that second threshold constitute a Tier 2 deficit.

Under the current draft text, these two deficits cannot be balanced in the same way. Tier 1 must be covered by Tier 1 RUs, while transferred or banked surplus units can be used to address Tier 2 deficits alongside Tier 2 RUs. Surplus trading can therefore reduce the cost of non-compliance with the Base Target, but it cannot substitute for the entire economic signal between the Direct Compliance and Base thresholds.

This gives the IMO model a different character from a single-threshold system. Once the two targets diverge, a large supply of cheap surplus cannot simply satisfy the full compliance requirement of every higher-emitting vessel. The Tier 1 band remains linked to the remedial mechanism and consequently provides a source of demand for RUs even where the transferable surplus market is well supplied.

Note that Brazil’s proposed introductory period temporarily weakens that distinction because the two targets are identical in 2029 and 2030. There is effectively no Tier 1 band during those years. That makes the initial market particularly relevant when comparing the IMO design with the experience under FuelEU Maritime, because the first two years could allow a larger amount of relatively inexpensive surplus to enter the system before the more restrictive two-tier structure takes effect.

Remedial Units provide certainty when physical compliance or surplus is unavailable

Unlike a surplus unit, which originates from another vessel’s physical over-performance, an RU is obtained through a financial contribution to the IMO mechanism. Brazil argues that RUs should guarantee an adequate supply of compliance units and make the cost of meeting the regulation sufficiently predictable for shipping companies.

The original draft framework circulated in 2025 set initial prices of USD 100/tCO₂eq for Tier 1 RUs and USD 380/tCO₂eq for Tier 2 RUs for reporting periods 2028 to 2030, with IMO subsequently required to establish the mechanism for prices from 2031 onward. Brazil’s contribution does not itself replace those prices, although its proposal to shift the implementation timetable means that the corresponding years would need to be adjusted in the final legal text.

For the transferable market, the Tier 2 RU price is to be particularly important because it provides an alternative to purchasing another ship’s surplus units. Provided RUs remain readily available, a buyer has little reason to pay materially more for a Surplus Unit than the equivalent remedial compliance would cost. The RU price can therefore provide an effective upper reference point for surplus.

The reverse does not apply. The availability of a USD 380 remedial option does not mean that surplus units will trade anywhere close to USD 380. If surplus is abundant, its market price can fall towards the marginal cost of creating the next unit. The development of FuelEU over the past year provides a useful demonstration of exactly this effect.

FuelEU already shows how quickly a compliance market can find the cheapest solution

The first FuelEU Maritime compliance cycle provides an unusually relevant comparison because it combines a GHG-intensity target with banking, pooling and a financial fallback. Data from a forthcoming European Commission report shows that more than 90% of ships used pooling for the 2025 compliance year, while fewer than 2% used borrowing. Around 7% made no flexibility request, approximately half of that group complied directly and the remainder paid the FuelEU penalty.

From the perspective of regulatory compliance, this is an important result. A very large number of companies were able to match positive and negative compliance balances rather than relying on the statutory penalty, indicating that a market for over-compliance can become functional quickly. It also illustrates why flexibility is commercially attractive: a company does not necessarily need to decarbonise every vessel independently when lower-cost reductions can be sourced elsewhere in the market.

The fuel outcome is more nuanced. The same Commission data indicates that biofuel represented more than two-thirds of the renewable and low-carbon energy used for FuelEU compliance, while its modelling suggests that existing LNG use may have provided roughly one-third of the overall emissions reduction required in 2025. More capital-intensive options such as e-fuels, onshore power, and wind-assisted propulsion remained a small part of the compliance mix.

That demonstrates something fundamental about market-based fuel standards: when different pathways create the same fungible compliance value, the market tends to favour the cheapest available source first.

Current FuelEU pricing makes this effect particularly visible

The development of the FuelEU surplus market during 2026 provides an even clearer illustration. BetterSea’s transaction data shows that weighted end-of-month surplus prices reached €83.13/tCO₂e at the end of August 2026, with the weighted monthly average for August at €108.89/tCO₂e. This is materially below the values around €190-200/tCO₂e observed across parts of the first compliance cycle.

The fall in surplus prices has occurred alongside a fundamental change in the cost of generating new compliance. The Strait of Hormuz shock sharply increased conventional bunker prices while the increase in some biofuel prices was less pronounced, compressing the normal premium between fossil and renewable fuels. Several industry sources frequently reported during 2026 that FuelEU abatement costs considering biofuel and MGO fell below zero, meaning that under the relevant assumptions the biofuel switch is already economically advantageous before any positive value is assigned to the resulting FuelEU surplus.

This changes the composition of the surplus market. A company that previously purchased surplus because using alternative fuel was more expensive may now find that replacing MGO with an eligible biofuel is attractive on the underlying fuel and EU ETS economics alone. When more companies reach that conclusion, new supply enters the surplus market at a very low marginal generation cost and places downward pressure on the price.

The consequence is particularly challenging for fuels with higher production costs. A company using a more advanced alternative fuel may require a relatively high compliance value to compensate for the physical fuel premium, but it sells the same unit of FuelEU over-compliance as a company whose biofuel switch happened to generate surplus at almost no additional cost. The surplus market does not distinguish between those generation costs. Unless there is an additional fuel-specific support mechanism, the cheapest marginal supplier increasingly determines the market value received by every generator.

LNG and banking add a second source of surplus pressure

FuelEU also shows how existing fleet characteristics can contribute surplus without a new renewable-fuel investment. Fossil LNG can remain below the FuelEU GHG-intensity target depending on engine technology and methane slip.

The commercial treatment of this surplus differs between companies. A charterer controlling an LNG-fuelled vessel for a limited period may have little interest in preserving the compliance position of that ship ten years later and can instead monetise the current surplus through pooling. An owner and operator may reach the opposite conclusion and bank the positive balance to hedge against the vessel’s future FuelEU exposure. One can assume that a meaningful amount of surplus was retained rather than immediately monetised, although the publicly available first-year figures reviewed here do not provide an aggregate figure for the amount of surplus that was banked.

This matters because FuelEU banking has no expiry date. Positive compliance balances can be carried forward successively and banked surplus does not expire. A ship can therefore accumulate positive balances during relatively easy early compliance years and use that stock against considerably more stringent requirements later.

From a market perspective, this creates an additional layer of uncertainty. The surplus currently offered for pooling represents only part of the potential supply. Another part may sit in company accounts as banked compliance and return to the market or be consumed internally many years later. As the market develops, the size of this accumulated stock becomes increasingly relevant to any assessment of future supply, pricing and the marginal incentive for new alternative-fuel consumption.

The IMO architecture limits indefinite surplus accumulation

This is one area where the IMO draft takes a materially different (better) approach. A surplus unit would be valid for only two calendar years after the calendar year in which it was issued. If the unit remains unused when that period expires, it is cancelled as a mitigation contribution.

The rule does not prevent short-term oversupply. If market conditions make physical over-compliance unusually cheap, the fleet could still generate a large amount of surplus and depress prices for the following reporting periods. What the expiry mechanism prevents is the creation of an indefinitely growing stock of legacy compliance capable of competing with future physical decarbonisation many years later.

Combined with the rising Direct Compliance Target, that should make the market more responsive to current fuel economics. Surplus generated cheaply under an early and relatively weak target will eventually disappear, while new units will have to be produced against increasingly demanding GFI thresholds. This does not guarantee a high surplus unit price, but it reduces the risk that accumulated early over-compliance suppresses the market indefinitely.

The Direct Compliance Target provides a second safeguard. Once the Base and Direct Compliance targets diverge, a ship must achieve the deeper threshold before it generates transferable surplus. A vessel that simply meets the Base Target may avoid Tier 2 exposure, but it still has to deal with the Tier 1 deficit. This limits the extent to which inexpensive surplus from another ship can substitute for progressively improving the fleet’s GHG intensity.

The introductory period could nevertheless resemble FuelEU

Brazil’s proposed treatment of 2029 and 2030 makes the first two years more exposed to the same market dynamics now visible under FuelEU. With the Base and Direct Compliance targets both set at 3% in 2029 and 4% in 2030, there would effectively be no Tier 1 band. A vessel beating that single threshold could generate surplus, while a vessel above it would face the corresponding deficit without the stronger separation introduced from 2031 onward.

Whether this produces large quantities of low-cost surplus will depend heavily on the final well-to-wake GHG factors. Some LNG configurations could potentially perform favourably against an early target, while unexpected market movements could again (or still) make biofuel-based compliance unusually inexpensive. In that situation, a significant amount of surplus could be generated early on.

The crucial difference from FuelEU is that the effect would be temporary. Units cannot remain in circulation indefinitely. Still one may argue that an already delayed IMO NZF should not further soften the market.

ZNZ rewards address a problem that surplus trading cannot solve on its own

The FuelEU experience also explains why the separate zero- and near-zero, or ZNZ, reward mechanism is important. If all over-compliance is fungible, the ordinary surplus price will tend towards the cost of the cheapest available generator. That price may be sufficient to support a biodiesel blend or an existing LNG vessel but likely entirely insufficient to bridge the cost gap for e-methanol, e-ammonia, renewable hydrogen or other more capital-intensive pathways.

The draft IMO framework therefore separates ordinary compliance value from additional support for qualifying ZNZ fuels and technologies. Under the existing draft, the initial ZNZ threshold is set at no more than 19 gCO₂eq/MJ and becomes more stringent later in the trajectory. Brazil does not propose removing this mechanism. On the contrary, the operational model illustrated in its submission retains a dedicated ZNZ Rewards Window, through which payments could be made following evidence that qualifying zero- or near-zero fuels, technologies or energy sources had actually been used.

Surplus units would reward performance relative to the GFI compliance standard and allow efficient trading between ships. ZNZ rewards would have a different function: providing an additional economic signal to the technologies capable of delivering the much deeper reductions required later in the transition.

The effectiveness of this approach will depend on the detailed reward methodology and the available funding. A dedicated window does not in itself guarantee that an expensive fuel will become competitive, and Brazil recognises that substantial guideline work remains. It specifically identifies the calculation of GFI and ZNZ rewards, Facility governance and auditing, and sustainable-fuel certification as priority workstreams requiring greater clarity.

A lighter Facility rather than a large IMO Fund

The institutional design of the economic mechanism represents the second major area of compromise. Some IMO Member States have objected to establishing a substantial fund administered directly through IMO, while others have argued that revenue collection and redistribution are necessary if the framework is to support ZNZ deployment and an equitable transition. Brazil’s proposal attempts to preserve those functions without requiring IMO to perform all of the financial-management activities itself.

Instead of an IMO Net-Zero Fund, Brazil proposes exploring an IMO Facility. IMO would establish the governing rules, eligibility criteria and policy direction, but accredited international, regional or national financial institutions could undertake much of the practical implementation. Brazil describes this as a more streamlined mechanism focused on collecting and deploying revenue through established implementing institutions, which would report back to IMO and operate according to its guidelines. The Facility could also be temporary and include a sunset clause. Financial contributions associated with deficit balancing, together with possible voluntary donations, would flow into the Facility. One channel would finance ZNZ rewards, while a separate Just & Equitable Transition Window would finance eligible projects through international, regional or national financial institutions.

The proposal seeks to reduce the need for IMO itself to become a large-scale asset manager, project evaluator and financing institution, addressing one of the major counter arguments posed against the previous draft.

A cheap surplus market could also affect the amount of money reaching the Facility

There is, however, an interaction between surplus prices and Facility funding that deserves attention. Where a Tier 2 deficit can be balanced either with a traded surplus unit or a Tier 2 RU, companies will naturally choose the less expensive route. If physical over-compliance becomes cheap and the market is well supplied with surplus units, fewer Tier 2 RUs may be purchased and less revenue may flow into the Facility. A similar behavorial pattern was observed in FuelEU Maritime when comparing the uptake of pooling vs paying the penalty, as discussed above.

The two-tier structure partly limits that effect. Once the Base and Direct Compliance Targets separate, Tier 1 deficits continue to require RUs and therefore create a more stable source of financial contributions irrespective of Tier 2 surplus availability. Brazil also proposes permitting voluntary donations.

Nevertheless, the relationship between RU demand and the size of the ZNZ reward pool will need careful consideration when the guidelines are developed. If the framework relies on compliance contributions to support expensive zero- and near-zero fuels, it must remain capable of funding those rewards even when ordinary Tier 2 compliance becomes inexpensive. FuelEU demonstrates that market conditions can change the marginal cost of compliance much faster than long-term fuel-production projects can adjust.

Better transparency could become another advantage of the IMO model

A further lesson from FuelEU concerns market visibility. FuelEU allows unlimited banking, but the publicly available first-year compliance data provides much better information on the use of pooling and borrowing than on the aggregate stock of positive balances retained for the future. For market participants trying to assess supply and demand several years ahead, the amount of surplus already accumulated is an important variable.

The IMO GFI Registry should provide a stronger basis for transparency and is capable of the same as surplus unit issuance, transfer, banking, cancellation and expiry would all take place within a central system. The existing draft also foresees reporting to MEPC on the operation of the compliance mechanism.

The usefulness of that information will ultimately depend on the disclosure rules adopted in the supporting guidelines. If the market can see aggregate surplus issuance, transfers, vintage distribution and upcoming expiries, companies will be better able to assess the balance between existing supply and future demand. A compliance market in which a substantial quantity of banked surplus is invisible to participants would be considerably harder to predict efficiently (as currently seen in FuelEU Maritime), despite neccessary to drive long-term investments.

What FuelEU tells us about the Brazilian proposal

The first FuelEU cycle offers a useful way of assessing the design. It demonstrates that flexible compliance can work, that companies can create an active market for positive compliance balances and that only a comparatively small proportion of vessels need to rely on the expensive statutory fallback when sufficient surplus is available. At the same time, it shows that this success does not automatically translate into broad deployment of the most advanced fuels.

The development of 2026 prices makes the structural issue clearer. Once market disruption reduced the cost of switching from MGO to biofuel, companies that would previously have purchased compliance could become low-cost surplus generators themselves. Additional supply then placed downward pressure on surplus prices, weakening the revenue available to more expensive generators. BetterSea’s August weighted end-of-month price of €83.13/tCO₂e illustrates how far the market has moved from levels around €190-200/tCO₂e seen during the earlier compliance cycle.

The Brazilian version of the IMO framework (just as the previous draft) contains several features that could reduce the persistence of the same problem. Surplus expires after two years rather than remaining banked indefinitely. From 2031, surplus is generated against a substantially more stringent Direct Compliance Target rather than the Base Target. Tier 1 compliance cannot be purchased from the ordinary surplus unit market, preserving demand for the remedial mechanism. Finally, ZNZ fuels and technologies receive a separate reward channel rather than being expected to compete solely on the price of generic compliance.

None of these mechanisms eliminates the underlying market effect. If one pathway can generate an IMO Surplus Unit at very low cost, it will put downward pressure on the value of every other transferable surplus unit. The 2029 and 2030 introductory period may be particularly exposed because the two GFI thresholds are temporarily identical. The difference is that the IMO architecture does not rely on surplus trading alone to carry the entire decarbonisation incentive. It separates flexible compliance, remedial compliance and support for deep decarbonisation into different parts of the system.

That distinction may ultimately be one of the most important lessons from FuelEU. A compliance market is naturally designed to find the cheapest way to meet a regulatory target; it is not automatically designed to create a business case for every fuel pathway that will eventually be required. A regulatory framework that wants to achieve both objectives needs to distinguish between the value of ordinary compliance and the additional support required to move technologies down the cost curve.

Next steps at IMO

ISWG-GHG 22 did not agree on Brazil’s proposal or select a single revised architecture. The official outcome records the Chair’s observation that delegations showed willingness to continue working towards text that could be presented to MEPC 85, while interested Member States were invited to consult further and submit proposals reflecting greater convergence. Work on several of the implementation guidelines was also deferred because of time constraints.

The next formal negotiating stage is ISWG-GHG 23 from 23 to 27 November 2026, immediately ahead of MEPC 85 from 30 November to 3 December. The adjourned second extraordinary session of MEPC is then scheduled to resume on 4 December 2026, subject to confirmation by MEPC 85.

Brazil argues that the mid-term measures should be adopted no later than MEPC 85 and notes that the possible amendments have already been circulated through Circular Letter No. 5214 to satisfy the relevant MARPOL circulation requirements. It also proposes that the wider review of the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy should begin only after sufficient implementation experience exists, suggesting a review 16 months after entry into force of the mid-term measures.

title: How ethanol is expanding shipping’s fuel choices
summary: Despite new hype around ethanol as a "green" marine fuel, its actual emissions reduction potential remains questionable while dirty ships continue to burn excessive HFO. Mining giant VALE's plans for ethanol-powered vessels by 2029 are undermined by their simultaneous intent to retain conventional fossil fuel capability in "tri-fuel" conversions. This future-focused strategy offers no immediate solution for current excessive carbon intensity or impending FuelEU Maritime penalties for the existing fleet.
content:
Ethanol is beginning to gain momentum as a viable option for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in shipping. A growing number of projects and technical developments are helping to move the fuel from regional discussions to global considerations.

For years, ethanol sat on the periphery of the maritime fuel debate. Whilst the orderbook shows that LNG and, more recently, methanol have seen growing uptake in the global fleet, ethanol has remained largely confined to regional discussions despite being the world’s most widely produced liquid biofuel.

That picture is beginning to change.

Why interest is growing in ethanol as marine fuel

Part of ethanol’s appeal is its maturity outside shipping. Decades of use in road transport have created extensive production capacity, established supply chains, and well-developed fuel logistics. At the same time, increasing focus on lifecycle emissions and regulations such as FuelEU Maritime are directing attention towards fuels capable of delivering meaningful well-to-wake greenhouse gas reductions.

However, production scale and emissions performance alone do not explain the growing interest. Ethanol is entering the maritime conversation at a time when the industry is searching for practical pathways that can support decarbonization without locking companies into a single long-term fuel choice.

Why cargo owners are investing in ethanol-powered ships

Among those exploring ethanol’s potential is VALE, a mining company and cargo owner which sees the fuel as part of its broader decarbonization strategy.

That commitment is already translating into projects. VALE has partnered with Shandong Shipping to build at least two Guaibamax vessels equipped with rotor sails and powered by ethanol, with delivery expected in 2029, and is evaluating the conversion of methanol-fuelled vessels into tri-fuel ships capable of operating on methanol, ethanol, and conventional fuel.

For VALE, a central focus of these projects is how they support the company in maintaining flexibility, thus creating options in an uncertain market. This reflects a broader industry trend towards preserving fuel flexibility whilst continuing to reduce emissions.

“Designing and constructing new ships is the most cost-effective and integrated opportunity to incorporate technological advances in our decarbonization program,” says Rodrigo Bermelho, Shipping Director at VALE. “This approach provides flexibility during regulatory and market uncertainty, enabling VALE to advance decarbonization whilst maintaining different strategic options.”

Shared technology, greater flexibility: the growing ethanol–methanol opportunity

One of the most interesting aspects of ethanol’s emergence is that it is not developing in isolation.

The fuel enters the maritime conversation at a time when investments in methanol technology are accelerating. The two alcohol fuels share several characteristics, creating opportunities to build on existing engine developments, fuel systems, and operational experience rather than requiring a completely separate technological pathway.

“Ethanol shares some characteristics with methanol and may offer additional flexibility for certain vessel applications over time,” says Mario Barbosa, General Manager Latin America at Wärtsilä.

This connection could prove important as shipowners seek to maintain flexibility in an increasingly uncertain fuel landscape. Rather than committing to a single fuel pathway, they may be able to leverage technologies and vessels capable of accommodating multiple future fuel options.

Ethanol requires own technical assessment

Whilst the similarities between methanol and ethanol create opportunities, industry experts stress that the two fuels should not be treated identically. Safety considerations also remain important. However, ethanol benefits from the fact that alcohol fuels are already covered by established IMO safety frameworks, whilst growing operational experience with methanol is helping the industry better understand the safe handling and use of alcohol-based marine fuels.

“Engine parameters, fuel injection, fuel system specifications, and safety considerations need to be carefully assessed for each vessel and application,” says Barbosa. “Ethanol brings its own characteristics, including differences in energy content, which means optimization is important to support reliable and efficient operation.”

In practice, this means that ethanol benefits from lessons learned through methanol adoption but still requires its own technical assessment. Fuel system design, engine configuration, and operational requirements must all be considered when evaluating ethanol for a specific vessel or trade.

New vessel designs keep fuel options open in an uncertain market

The growing link between ethanol and methanol is already influencing vessel design decisions.

According to Jones Soares, Shipping Operations Director at Transpetro, new vessels are increasingly being specified with the flexibility to use both conventional fuels and biofuels such as ethanol.

In May 2026, the dual-fuel container feeder vessel “Eco Levant” bunkered ethanol at Rotterdam for the first time, which it uses in a blend with 90 per cent bio-methanol.

“There is an intense debate within the maritime sector regarding the most effective solutions to meet the decarbonization standards stipulated by the IMO,” says Soares. “In this regard, the new vessels we’re commissioning are designed to use both traditional fuels and biofuels, such as ethanol, which is produced on a large scale in Brazil.”

“From an operational standpoint, the technology for methanol-powered vessels is already available and fully functional. Since both alcohols are similar, only minor software and engine modifications are required to operate using ethanol.”

Economics and availability will determine scale of ethanol

Such developments and the growing number of projects and vessels specifications suggest the conversation around ethanol is moving beyond the conceptual stage. The next question is whether ethanol can compete economically and be supplied at scale. However, wider adoption will still depend on factors such as fuel availability, bunkering infrastructure, regulatory treatment, and economics.

“The relevant question is no longer simply the cost of the fuel but the cost of reducing emissions, whilst maintaining regulatory compliance,” says Jason Stefanatos, Global Decarbonization Director at DNV Maritime. “In that context, fuels such as ethanol may become increasingly attractive where they can deliver meaningful greenhouse-gas reductions whilst leveraging existing infrastructure, technologies, and supply chains.”

Availability will be equally important. Although ethanol production is already substantial, future uptake will depend on the industry’s ability to make fuel available where and when it is needed through marine-specific supply chains and bunkering infrastructure, which remain in the early stages of development. According to Brazil’s Energy Research Office (EPE), ethanol production in Brazil could reach 51 billion litres by 2035, around 30% higher than current production levels. Improving visibility of this growing supply base is also becoming a priority. DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight (AFI) platform recently launched a three-year data intelligence partnership with the Global Ethanol Association to build a structured database of ethanol production facilities, feedstocks and fuel availability, helping the industry better assess ethanol’s potential as a marine fuel.

Understanding the sustainability of ethanol across different production pathways

As interest in ethanol grows, so too does scrutiny of how it is produced. Like many biofuels, ethanol sits at the centre of a long-running debate around land use, water use, and competition with food production.

According to Flavio Haruo Mathuiy, former Brazilian Navy captain and member of Brazil’s coordination commission for IMO affairs, these discussions are important to ensure that biofuels are produced in a sustainable way. Historically, the production of Brazilian sugarcane ethanol has always been tied to sugar – an essential food staple and a key input for the food and biotechnology industries. Likewise, and more recently, corn ethanol production has been associated with by-products destined for animal feed, such as dried distillers grains (DDG) and corn oil.

“The food-versus-fuel discussion cannot be viewed in isolation,” he says. “Different production pathways have very different sustainability characteristics, and in Brazil, ethanol production is increasingly linked to integrated agricultural systems, co-products, and food production simultaneously that can reduce pressure on food supplies whilst delivering significant emissions reductions.”

Mathuiy argues that assessing ethanol’s sustainability requires a lifecycle perspective that considers how and where the fuel is produced, rather than treating all ethanol pathways as equal.

Regulation will shape the future uptake of ethanol

Technology, fuel availability, and sustainability alone will not determine ethanol’s future role in shipping. How different production pathways are treated under regulatory frameworks may prove just as important.

Recent progress at IMO, together with incentives created by regional frameworks such as FuelEU Maritime, which include the recognition of specific ethanol pathways within lifecycle assessment discussions, has helped strengthen confidence in the fuel’s potential role. However, wider adoption will require continued alignment between IMO requirements, regional regulations, and sustainability certification systems.

According to Mathuiy, achieving greater harmonization between these frameworks will be essential if ethanol is to compete effectively with other low-GHG fuel options. Ultimately, the competitiveness of ethanol may depend not only on how the fuel is produced, but also on how those production pathways are recognized under future lifecycle emissions methodologies and compliance regimes.

Can ethanol scale as a marine fuel for shipping decarbonization?

Like other alternative fuels, ethanol faces both opportunities and challenges as a decarbonization pathway. Questions remain around infrastructure, sustainability, and regulation, and its future role will depend on how these challenges evolve.

Yet momentum is clearly building. As the orderbook shows, real-world projects are moving forward, ethanol is appearing in vessel specifications, and growing experience with methanol is helping to lower some of the barriers to adoption.

title: Study: Shipping is Off Track for 2030 Emissions Goals
summary: A new UCL study confirms the shipping industry is severely off track for its 2030 alternative fuel targets, ensuring sustained high carbon intensity across the fleet. Regulatory failure, specifically the IMO's Net-Zero Framework indecision, directly incentivizes continued reliance on heavy fuel oil (HFO) and will lead to increased FuelEU Maritime fines. Despite minor advancements like increased methanol bunkering ports, the industry already missed its 2025 milestone for 100 large zero-emission vessels, exposing a clear lack of tangible decarbonization efforts.
content:
The shipping industry will likely miss its 2030 targets for vessels running on alternative fuels, according to a new study from the UCL Energy Institute, mainly due to the regulatory uncertainties surrounding the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF).

According to the fifth edition of 'Climate action in shipping: Progress towards shipping's 2030 breakthrough', the industry is highly unlikely to meet targets of having zero-emission fuels accounting for 5-10 percent of total fuel usage, the goal set in the 2023 IMO Greenhouse Gas Strategy. The ultimate goal is to ensure the shipping industry becomes net-zero by 2050, and the 2030 target was conceived as an enabler to accelerate early progress.

The 2030 targets meant that some 600-1,200 large ships with a capacity of at least 15,000 TEU (or equivalent) would be running on scalable zero-emissions fuels (SZEF). However, owing to headwinds like economic and political upheaval, the Strait of Hormuz crisis, energy security and supply chain concerns, and the regulatory uncertainty caused by the failure to adopt the NZF, the world is lagging behind on its alternative fuel goals. In 2025, the milestone of having roughly 100 15,000-TEU-equivalent ships running on SZEF was not met.

The UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition report shows that while the world is falling behind on its goals, there have been notable achievements across the five key 'levers' being used to assess the industry's progress - namely technology and supply, demand, finance, policy, and civil society.

Supply of alternative fuels and technologies has, for instance, been progressing. The number of ports offering methanol bunkering now stands at 29, up from 19 a year ago. The world has also witnessed sea trials of the first large ammonia-fueled vessels with two-stroke engines being successfully completed, as well as the building of smaller ammonia-fueled supply vessels and tugboats fitted with four-stroke engines. The industry has also recorded its first ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering operation.

The report shows that the long-anticipated wave of methanol-capable container ship deliveries finally landed in 2025, tripling methanol-capable in-service tonnage from 2.3 million to 7.7 million gross tonnage (GT) and pushing the SZEF-capable share of the active fleet from 0.41 percent to 0.77 percent. This was the largest single-year capability gain on record, delivered through 56 newbuilds totaling 5.4 million GT. However, the order book regressed, with SZEF-capable orders falling from 9.5 percent to 5.7 percent of total GT orders.

On finance, the progress has been mixed: issuances of shipping-specific sustainable debt have plateaued. In 2025, approximately $3 billion was issued to shipping-related entities through green loans, green bonds, sustainability-linked loans, and transition instruments, down from $3.4 billion in 2024.

For the industry, the controversies surrounding the NZF have become one of the major roadblocks towards the 2030 goals, with the U.S. being among its staunchest opponents. The report reckons that with the NZF remaining in limbo, the policy clarity required for the 2030 goal is a major obstacle.
