She added that reversing this momentum loss and securing regulatory certainty is one of the most important next steps to give shipowners the confidence to order zero-emission vessels, lenders the incentive to invest in them, and charterers the motivation to pay for low-carbon shipping.

title: IMO targets alternative fuel spill response
summary: While the IMO convenes forums on future alternative fuel spill response, the industry's pervasive reliance on high-carbon HFO continues unabated. This pre-emptive focus on hypothetical incidents for cleaner fuels conveniently deflects from the urgent need to mitigate current, measurable carbon intensity from the existing dirty fleet. dirtiestships.com demands immediate, tangible action on FuelEU Maritime fines and the excessive HFO consumption driving current emissions, not just future contingencies for fuels barely adopted.
content:
Participants at an International Maritime Organization (IMO) forum have called for greater cooperation to address gaps in spill-response preparedness as shipping expands its use of alternative bunker fuels.

The IMO’s two-day research and development forum, held in Singapore on 21–22 September, examined how the different properties of LNG, LPG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen and biofuels could affect marine pollution incidents and emergency response operations.

Participants stressed that spill-response measures need to keep up with the shift to alternative bunker fuels, and that procedures should be in place for each fuel before major incidents occur.

The participants also examined how the behaviour of each fuel in a spill could change the way responders handle an incident.

They called for closer cooperation between governments, industry and researchers to ensure that ongoing research and operational experience inform future spill-response protocols.

title: China seizes PCTC orders as Europe pivots, South Korea targets LNG carriers
summary: China's surging automobile exports have triggered a massive PCTC ordering spree, with Chinese shipyards securing 56 of 58 global orders this year. This rapid fleet expansion, alarmingly including the high-value trade of a 26-year-old PCTC, prioritizes immediate capacity over crucial decarbonisation efforts. Without immediate and stringent adoption of low-carbon fuels and technologies, this surge guarantees a substantial rise in maritime emissions and future FuelEU Maritime compliance headaches.
content:
China’s solo dominance is hardening in the global pure car and truck carrier (PCTC) ordering market. As China’s automobile export volumes surge and Chinese shipbuilders absorb the carrier demand, European shipping companies that had assigned work to Korea and others are also said to have recently placed large-scale orders in China.

According to Clarksons Research, a British shipbuilding and shipping market analysis firm, 58 new PCTCs were ordered worldwide from the start of the year through last month. China won orders for 56 of them.

In 2023 and 2024, PCTC orders were 83 and 73 ships, respectively, but amid concerns about oversupply last year, orders plunged to nine. However, this year, as China’s automobile exports increased, projections grew that there were not enough ships to transport them, expanding PCTC demand again.

According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), in the first half of this year China exported 5,096,000 vehicles, up 65.3% from the same period a year earlier. In June alone, auto exports reached 1,037,000, surpassing 1 million for the first time.

While China’s automobile export volumes have surged, PCTC supply is short, and demand for secondhand vessels has also increased sharply. In July, a 26-year-old 4,310 CEU-class PCTC in China sold for about $42 million, three times the minimum bid price of about $14 million. One CEU is space for one car, and the ship was a mid-sized PCTC capable of carrying about 4,300 passenger cars.

China’s auto industry has remarked on a shortage of carriers. According to Reuters and other foreign media, executives at Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD said on this month’s first-half earnings conference call that “overseas exports were hampered by transport constraints this year,” adding, “if transport had been smooth, exports would have been higher.”

As PCTC demand rose, Chinese automakers and shipping companies signed construction contracts with domestic shipyards to secure their fleets. According to Greek maritime outlet Loban Asaphina, BYD this month ordered 10 9,200 CEU-class PCTCs from a Chinese shipyard. China-registered Hong Kong carrier Zhongnan Shipping is also said to have ordered four PCTCs in July from Jiangsu New Yangzi Shipbuilding in Jiangsu province.

Overseas carriers are also expanding their fleets. This year, European carriers have signed 33 construction contracts with Chinese shipyards. The company that ordered the most ships among them is Italy’s Grimaldi, which ordered a total of 12 PCTCs from three Chinese shipbuilders.

The concentration of PCTC orders from Chinese and overseas carriers at Chinese shipbuilders is not just due to strong price competitiveness. Because PCTCs do not require cutting-edge technology, construction demand flows to places that can build at lower unit costs. The fact that Korean shipyards’ docks are saturated with large container ships and liquefied natural gas carriers (LNGCs) is also cited as a factor concentrating orders in China.

China’s policy stance of protecting domestic supply chains also played a role. China is supporting ship finance to encourage domestic carriers and automakers to place orders with Chinese shipyards. Eom Kyung-a, an analyst at Shinyoung Securities, said, “For the purpose of using ship finance, many Chinese carriers place orders with domestic shipyards.”

Carriers that had ordered PCTCs only from Korean shipbuilders have recently chosen China. Under China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), China Shipbuilding Trading Company signed a contract to build ten 8,200 CEU-class PCTCs with Israeli shipowner Ray Car Carriers. Ray Car Carriers has placed PCTC orders only in Korea for the past 20 years. In April this year, the company also ordered two PCTCs from HD Hyundai Heavy Industries.

title: New research shows how regulation could reshape shipping
summary: DNV's latest Maritime Forecast to 2050 emphasizes "regulatory uncertainty" as the primary driver shaping future fleet strategies and fuel choices. While "technology options are increasingly well understood," this report focuses on various regulatory scenarios rather than immediate, concrete action. Such academic exercises offer little to address the shipping industry's current excessive HFO consumption or the urgent need for stringent FuelEU Maritime compliance to curb actual carbon intensity.
content:
Amid regulatory uncertainty, there is one key challenge to ensuring shipping meets its decarbonization goals: making the right decisions today. DNV’s latest edition of Maritime Forecast to 2050 explores how different scenarios could reshape fuel demand, investment decisions, and decarbonization pathways, helping shipowners to navigate uncertainty and build resilient fleets.

Shipping’s energy transition has entered a new phase. The technology options are increasingly well understood. LNG, methanol, biofuels, wind-assisted propulsion, and emerging ammonia solutions are no longer concepts but commercial realities. Yet despite this progress, shipowners face a more difficult challenge than ever: making investment decisions amid unprecedented regulatory uncertainty.

The 2026 edition of DNV’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 argues that uncertainty itself is now becoming one of the most important drivers of fleet strategy. “Decisions taken today on vessel design, retrofits, and fuel capability will determine competitiveness for decades, while the outcome of ongoing regulatory negotiations could significantly reshape the economics of shipping’s energy transition,” says Øyvind Sekkesæter, Senior Consultant at DNV and lead author of this year’s report. “Maritime Forecast to 2050 aims to assist that decision-making with our latest core insights and case study examples.”

Four regulatory scenarios could shape shipping very differently

This year’s Maritime Forecast takes a scenario-based approach, presenting four possible regulatory futures for shipping. These range from the full adoption of IMO’s initially approved Net-Zero Framework (NZF) to its rejection and prolonged political gridlock, while also exploring several intermediate outcomes, including a delayed or revised NZF and scenarios where regional regulations play a more prominent role in driving decarbonization. Rather than predicting which outcome is most likely, the scenarios illustrate how different regulatory futures could affect fuel demand, energy-efficiency uptake, investment signals, and fleet competitiveness.

Stronger global regulation accelerates demand for low-GHG fuels and increases the attractiveness of energy-efficiency measures, while the absence of such regulation slows market development. The result is a transition whose pace may vary significantly depending on future policy decisions.

“For shipowners, this means the challenge is no longer identifying a single fuel pathway that fits the operational profile of their fleet. Instead, it is preparing fleets that remain competitive across multiple possible futures,” Sekkesæter concludes.

Tapping the fleet’s efficiency potential

Fully realizing the fleet’s energy-saving potential requires improvements not only to newbuilds but also to existing ships through retrofits.

Installing energy-saving devices during scheduled dry-docking can be a highly cost-effective decarbonization strategy, as illustrated by the Maritime Forecast’s case study of a hypothetical 15-year-old 5,000 TEU containership (built in 2013).

This envisages USD 2.35 million being invested to retrofit the ship with hydrodynamic enhancements including a bow retrofit, propeller upgrade, and a propeller boss cap fin.

The vessel can achieve estimated fuel savings of around 16% under the modelling assumptions. Evaluating the investment under three price scenarios for low sulphur heavy fuel oil (LSHFO) results in payback periods from 1.4 years to 4.2 years.

A USD 10 million opportunity: The business case for ship retrofits is strengthening

In the above scenarios, the net present value of the net savings is projected to reach between USD 2 and 10 million by 2038. The investment case is further strengthened by rising compliance costs under regulatory schemes such as the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and FuelEU Maritime, which were excluded from the baseline assumptions.

“The key takeaway from this study is that even a 15-year-old vessel can offer a compelling business case for retrofitting energy-saving measures. The report also reveals that, unlike fuel choices, efficiency improvements create value under every regulatory scenario,” highlights Sekkesæter. At fleet level, the implications are substantial.

Operational excellence and quantifying real-world performance

Of course, shipowners making multi-million-dollar investments need to be able to trust that the claimed benefits of equipment and measures are real.

Standardized measurements and verification are a solution. To bridge trust gaps, DNV’s Vessel Technical Index (VTI), introduced under Recommended Practice DNV-RP-0675, provides a normalized, dimensionless propulsion power index that isolates a ship’s technical performance from external factors like weather and speed.

Using the VTI can verify the impact of routine operational measures. The Maritime Forecast reports that for one chartered vessel, sensor data collected before and after hull and propeller cleaning showed a statistically significant VTI reduction from a mean of 1.32 down to 1.14 relative to an “as-new” baseline of 1.00.

This improvement saved approximately 120 tonnes of fuel over a 33-day voyage. At a fuel price of USD 470/tonne, this equated to USD 56,000 in fuel cost savings, four times more than the USD 14,000 cleaning cost.

Alternative fuel technology uptake is surging

In examining ship-fuel trends through the lens of market data, the Maritime Forecast finds a major shift underway in the global order book, with alternative-fuel-capable gross tonnage surging from just 0.4% in 2020 to 5.2% in 2026.

Uptake is highly segmented, driven by different commercial realities and trade routes. Car carriers see the highest share, with 26% being alternative-fuel-capable, followed by cruise ships (19%) and containerships (11%). Bulk carriers (1.1%) and tankers (1.2% to 5%) lag in part due to tramp trading patterns and uncertain bunkering availability.

DNV data shows LNG and methanol dominating alternative fuel systems, though their installed capacity is underutilized.

“Many dual-fuel ships continue to use conventional fuel oils because alternative fuels remain more expensive and regulatory incentives are limited. Their dual-fuel capability therefore provides future flexibility rather than guaranteeing daily use of alternative fuels,” Sekkesæter explains.

Estimating potential demand for low-GHG fuels

To project how these trends are shaping the maritime fuel transition, the Maritime Forecast estimates total potential demand for low-GHG fuels in shipping using two selected regulatory scenarios that bracket the range of possible outcomes for NZF, as shown in the figure below.

By 2050, maritime demand for low-GHG fuels could range from 33 Mtoe to 185 Mtoe depending on regulatory ambition and energy-efficiency uptake. However, total demand across all sectors could exceed 2,200 Mtoe under a net-zero pathway. Aviation, manufacturing, power generation, and road transport are all expected to compete for many of the same fuel molecules and feedstocks.

This competition is particularly intense for biofuels, which are currently among the most economically attractive decarbonization options. Because sustainable biomass availability is inherently limited, growing demand across sectors is likely to increase competition and put upward pressure on fuel costs. DNV’s analysis suggests that higher-cost pathways such as blue fuels and e-fuels will increasingly be needed to balance future demand.

A bottleneck for alternative fuel bunkering

For financiers and insurers evaluating vessel risk, and charterers planning voyages, fuel availability in ports remains a critical factor in determining fuel viability. Encouragingly, the global bunkering vessel fleet is expanding rapidly. Operational LNG bunkering vessels have risen from 25 in 2020 to 67 today, while 24 methanol bunkering vessels are operating and eight are on order. The first dedicated ammonia bunkering vessel recently entered the order book to operate in Singapore.

However, low-GHG fuel bunkering is highly concentrated along major European and East Asian trade routes. The Maritime Forecast also finds that while low-GHG bunkering has occurred at nearly 90 ports globally, the type of fuel available varies dramatically.

Biodiesels, including FAME and HVO, are the most mature and widely distributed, supplied at nearly 70 ports. Liquefied bio-methane is available at 20 ports, mainly in Europe. Low-GHG methanol has been bunkered at 16 ports, concentrated in East Asia and Western Europe. Low-GHG ammonia remains in its infancy, with bunkering reported at only three ports, all in East Asia.

title: Interferry: Unlock the Full Electrification Potential Through EU ETS
summary: Interferry welcomes the EU ETS revision, yet immediately preconditions widespread ferry electrification on massive public funding and urgently required shore power infrastructure. This highlights the glaring lack of current port grid capacity and shore power connections, effectively delaying meaningful carbon intensity reductions while ships continue burning fossil fuels. Their demand to ring-fence 100% of maritime ETS revenues for decarbonization reveals an industry seeking public subsidy for transitions that should be driven by urgent operational emission cuts, not future promises.
content:
Interferry, the global trade association representing the ferry industry, has welcomed the European Commission’s proposed revision of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The association says the proposal has significant potential to accelerate maritime decarbonization, provided the final text secures accessible onshore power infrastructure and reliable grid connections through Member State obligations and more robust funding mechanisms.

Interferry strongly supports the proposal’s alignment with the sector’s strategy to decarbonize through financially sustainable electrification of ports and vessels. However, expanding hybrid and battery-electric ferry operations depends on EU passenger ports fulfilling their legal obligations to provide onshore power supply (OPS). Member States must also ensure that local grids can deliver enough electricity for ports to charge hybrid and fully electric vessels without disrupting regional energy supplies.

To support this transition, Interferry is calling on lawmakers to ring-fence 100% of maritime ETS revenues for maritime decarbonization, including support for EU-produced sustainable marine fuels, clean technologies, and onshore charging infrastructure.

While Interferry welcomes the proposed Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism, it sees significant risk that demand will exceed the available funding: the estimated EUR 1 billion annually must support the entire maritime sector, including ferry shipping. Member States should therefore supplement SMAP funding with targeted national support.

Finally, the revision must establish a clear, predictable pathway for zero-emission operators to access SMAP funding in advance. Although operators of fully electric ferries surrender no allowances, they face substantial upfront capital costs.

“Ferry operators have led the way in electrification, but inadequate shore power and grid capacity limit the battery capacity they can put to use and, in turn, the distances they can cover. Larger batteries and longer crossings are technically feasible, and several large ro-pax ferries are already battery-ready. We are fulfilling our commitment, but ferry operators cannot resolve grid connection and other landside infrastructure issues on their own. Ports and Member States have a vital role to play, and the Commission’s proposal to revise the maritime EU ETS offers tools to help fund the necessary investment,” said Johan Roos, Director of Regulatory Affairs at Interferry.

title: President Trump Renews Attack on IMO NZF, Says 'No Global Taxes' While He Is President
summary: Donald Trump has renewed his staunch opposition to the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework, specifically targeting its proposed "global carbon tax" as an unacceptable cost burden. He warns that such a mechanism would inflate international shipping expenses by 10-20% and vows "no global taxes" during his presidency. This political posturing threatens to derail efforts to implement a critical economic mechanism designed to penalize carbon intensity and drive the shipping industry away from excessive high-carbon fuel consumption.
content:
Trump addresses United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. Image Credit: Department of Energy

US President Donald Trump has renewed his criticism of the IMO’s proposedNet-Zero Framework (NZF), calling its proposed emissions pricing mechanism a “global carbon tax”.

Trump made the remarks on Tuesday, during his address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

“Last year, my administration was forced to intervene to stop an obscure UN body, the International Maritime Organization, from secretly establishing a first-ever global carbon tax,” Trump said in his speech.

He claimed the measure would increase international shipping costs by 10-20%, “and maybe more than that”.

“There is no global government,” Trump said.

“And while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.”

The comments come as the NZF remains under consideration after member states postponed its formal adoption in October 2025.

Ahead of the October 2025 meeting, Trump said in a social media post that the US would not adhere to the framework in any way or form. At that time, his administration also warned of potential retaliation against countries supporting the framework.

Trump’s latest comments come as IMO member states prepare to meet again next month to discuss the framework and seek consensus, with the aim of adopting the proposal in December.

The NZF includes a global fuel standard and an economic mechanism designed to price greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping.

title: What happens when net zero becomes auditable?
summary: The impending ISO 14060 standard will finally scrutinize corporate net-zero claims, exposing shipping lines that merely announce targets without credible, verifiable transition plans. This directly challenges pervasive "greenwashing," where many companies disclose net-zero ambitions but fail to back them with tangible commitments, as evidenced by SBTi removing 239 non-compliant firms. For the maritime sector, future carbon intensity reductions and FuelEU Maritime compliance will demand independently verifiable action, not rhetoric, to avoid substantial financial penalties.
content:
Captain Alex Byelyavtsev is back with some uncomfortable predictions for some owners.

ISO’s public consultation on ISO 14060 closed on September 9, 2026. The draft is intended to become what ISO describes as the world’s first international independently verifiable standard for credible net-zero alignment. Final text is still ahead. The harder question for shipping is already here.

When net zero becomes auditable, are companies ready for verification – or mainly ready to announce a target? For years, net zero was primarily a statement of intent. Audibility turns it into a statement that has to survive evidence.

According to CDP, almost 6,000 companies disclosed having a 1.5°C-aligned climate transition plan in 2023. Only 140 disclosed sufficiently against all 21 of CDP’s credibility indicators, up from 81 the year before. ISO 14060 is built to close that gap by making plans comparable, not just visible. Two companies can name the same net-zero year. One may have interim targets, capital committed, supplier programmes and milestones. Another may have little more than a promise. From the outside, those plans can look identical until someone has to verify them.

ISO 14060 is not the IMO Net-Zero Framework. The IMO track is the proposed ship- and fuel-level regulatory architecture for the fleet. ISO 14060 asks whether a corporate net-zero claim, and the transition plan behind it, can stand independent check. Shipping sits in the path of both. Confusing them is how readiness gets misread.

The Science Based Targets initiative already showed what happens when a claim meets a validation gate. On 7 March 2024, SBTi marked 239 companies from its Business Ambition for 1.5°C campaign as “Commitment Removed.” Under the revised compliance policy, they had 24 months from when SBTi began validating against the Corporate Net-Zero Standard to submit targets, with a deadline of 31 January 2024, and did not clear that step. In SBTi’s campaign survey, 54% of respondents ranked Scope 3 as a barrier to setting a net-zero target. Sixty percent of the 239 still had near-term targets set. The net-zero commitment was the part that failed the evidence test. That was not a shipping regulation. It was a preview of auditable net zero. The announcement was easy. The package an assessor could check was not.

Shipping is ahead of most sectors on vessel data. The IMO data collection system, the Carbon Intensity Indicator, EU ETS for European port calls and FuelEU Maritime pushed monitoring, intensity, carbon cost and fuel choice into operations. Lines moved ships, bought different fuels and brought capital decisions forward because proof started to matter at ship level.

That stack is not an audit-ready corporate transition plan. Shipping may be data-rich at vessel level and still evidence-poor at corporate transition level. Vessel MRV can be strong while the company pathway still lacks checkable interim milestones, capital trails, fuel offtake evidence and Scope 3 data from bunker producers, traders and cargo counterparts.

Maersk is a useful case precisely because much of the evidence already exists. There are SBTi-validated targets, including a 96.2% absolute cut in well-to-wake Scope 1 and 3 emissions from container shipping operations by 2040 from a 2022 base year and a 90% absolute cut in Scope 3. There is methanol-capable tonnage. There are long-term fuel offtake agreements. Yet even a documented pathway still depends on physical conditions the company cannot create alone: sufficient fuel, in the right ports, at workable prices. A documented pathway is necessary for verification. It is not proof that the physical chain will work at scale.

Audibility is already landing where money moves. Cargo owners ask for Scope 3 data in tenders. Banks and lessors put transition questions into lending and asset risk. Charter clauses and bunker contracts carry fuel and emissions language that used to sit only in a sustainability report. ISO 14060 raises the evidence bar for the company making the claim. ISO 32212, published in early June 2026 shortly before the 14060 consultation opened, pushes transition discipline into the institutions financing it. Verification pressure comes from both ends: corporate claims and capital providers. Transition planning is moving out of the brochure and closer to the contracts, credit decisions and procurement processes where claims acquire consequences.

For many large companies, the majority of reported emissions sit in Scope 3. Asking suppliers for disclosures is rational. Verifying every supplier, contractor and fuel producer behind the claim is where SBTi’s validation cliff was steepest – and where ISO 14060 will meet the same limit.

The draft adds guidance for SMEs in an annex, without letting that guidance stand in for full conformity claims. Large firms usually have staff for audit packs. Smaller ones may find it harder to prove a target than to set one. That is not the main risk for shipping. The main risk is treating ship-level compliance systems as if they already equal a corporate plan an auditor can clear.

Net zero is becoming less a question of what a company says it will do, and more a question of what an independent third party can actually verify that it is doing. Shipping already knows what happens when regulation moves from declaration to measurement. The next test is harder: whether the corporate transition story can survive the same scrutiny.

title: Trump Takes Aim at IMO and the Net Zero Framework at the UN
summary: Former US President Trump's vocal opposition to the IMO's proposed global carbon price, framed as a "global tax," significantly undermines efforts to establish a robust economic mechanism for decarbonizing shipping. This political interference effectively stalls crucial steps towards holding high-emitting vessels accountable and incentivizing the long-overdue transition away from cheap, high-carbon HFO. Without a globally enforceable carbon price, the IMO's "net-zero by 2050" ambition remains largely aspirational, lacking the financial teeth to truly penalize excessive carbon intensity across global fleets.
content:
As the first global carbon price mechanism of any kind, the IMO Net Zero Framework's "economic measures" system has had its critics, and has attracted particular scrutiny from the Trump administration. The industry's proposed carbon agreement has even risen to the attention of the president, who used it in an address at the UN General Assembly as an example of the form of international regulation that he opposes.

"Last year, my administration was forced to intervene to stop an obscure UN body, the International Maritime Organization, from secretly establishing a first-ever global carbon tax - very expensive tax - to raise international shipping costs by 10 to 20 percent, and maybe even more than that," Trump claimed. "There is no global government, and while I'm president, there will be no global taxes."

Though it may be little-known outside of shipping circles, IMO has been working on CO2 for a long time. Member states first voted on a resolution to address CO2 emissions in 1997, and IMO has been implementing carbon regulations since the 2011 adoption of the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) standard. Though not a stringent regulation in itself, the EEDI demonstrated an industry consensus that ships should burn less fuel if possible, and that IMO could make rules designed to reduce carbon emissions.

IMO's member states followed up with their first "initial strategy" to regulate greenhouse gases in 2018, during the first Trump administration. After careful diplomacy, they agreed on an "ambition" to reduce emissions by 50% by midcentury.

Member states doubled that ambition five years later, adopting the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, which calls for net-zero emissions by 2050. The 2023 strategy added interim targets for 2030 and 2040. While not universally supported, it passed MEPC, setting the stage for debates on implementation - the real challenge, as achieving the ambition involves very real costs. Zero-carbon fuels are prohibitively expensive for market adoption, and as a practical matter, charterers and cargo interests have not shown a willingness to pay extra for green transport at scale. To truly scale up, bunker fuel prices would have to be forced upwards to level the playing field, create a market, and incentivize green-fuel producers and green-fueled shipowners to invest.

After considerable negotiation, in April 2025, member states tentatively agreed upon a "Net Zero Framework" with a set of "economic measures" at its core. This system is designed to achieve an economic goal: to collect revenue from ships that use more bunker fuel, raise the effective price of carbon-based bunkers, and use the collected funds to subsidize green fuel. Though the NZF is not categorized as a tax - it is a system of penalty fees based on fuel efficiency - it is expected to have a tax-like effect, creating a net IMO revenue stream of $10-15 billion per year.

That system has not yet been formally adopted, thanks in no small part to American opposition. The Trump administration views the NZF not as a narrow sectoral policy for shipowners, but as an initial step towards global carbon regulation for multiple industries. In October 2025, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy warned foreign governments that promoting the "activist-driven climate policies" in the IMO Net Zero Framework could result in sanctions, tariffs, new port fees or crew visa restrictions for states that backed the NZF. In a joint letter, they threatened to impose U.S. sanctions on individual foreign officials who supported the plan as well.

title: IMO Delay Puts Shipping’s 2030 Clean-Fuel Target Under Pressure
summary: The IMO's decision to postpone its Net-Zero Framework adoption to 2026 directly sabotages the 2030 decarbonization target, creating dangerous policy uncertainty. While methanol infrastructure and alternative fuel vessel technology advance, the industry's investment signals remain critically weak, not due to technical limits but a lack of commitment. This regulatory paralysis guarantees continued high carbon intensity from the global fleet, exposing operators to escalating FuelEU Maritime fines and dismal CII ratings.
content:
The shipping industry is making progress on alternative-fuel technology, but uncertainty over global regulation is threatening to slow investment needed to meet its 2030 decarbonization target.

Read also: World Shipping Council Urges IMO to Tighten Lithium Battery Cargo Rules

A 2025 assessment by the UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition found that developments in zero-emission fuel technology and supply are moving forward, while demand, financing and policy progress remain weaker. The report warns that these gaps could delay the industry’s 2030 breakthrough.

The issue centers on the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework. The framework was approved as draft regulations in April 2025, but formal adoption was postponed after IMO members adjourned discussions. The process is now scheduled to continue in 2026. (International Maritime Organization)

The proposed framework combines a global marine-fuel standard with a greenhouse-gas pricing mechanism. The measures are designed to reduce the emissions intensity of shipping fuels while creating financial incentives for the use of zero- and near-zero-emission alternatives. (International Maritime Organization)

Technology is advancing, but investment signals remain weak

The latest assessment points to a growing gap between what the industry can technically deploy and what companies are prepared to finance.

Methanol infrastructure has expanded, and more vessels are being built or adapted to use alternative fuels. The industry has also begun testing ammonia as a marine fuel.

However, the report’s five transition indicators show a less consistent picture. Technology and fuel supply are progressing, while demand and finance have not advanced at the same pace. Policy uncertainty is another major obstacle. (UCL Discovery)

That creates a difficult investment environment for shipowners, fuel producers, ports and financial institutions. Companies must make decisions on vessels and infrastructure that could remain in service for decades while the regulatory framework governing their emissions is still being finalized.

2030 target remains a key milestone

Under the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse-gas strategy, zero- or near-zero-emission technologies, fuels and energy sources are expected to account for at least 5%, with an ambition of 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030. The strategy also targets at least a 40% reduction in shipping’s carbon intensity by 2030 compared with 2008 and aims for net-zero greenhouse-gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. (International Maritime Organization)

The 5%-10% fuel target is therefore more than a standalone benchmark. It is intended to help establish the fuel markets and infrastructure needed for the industry’s longer-term transition.

The IMO says alternative zero- and near-zero-emission fuels will be critical to achieving its longer-term climate objectives. Its current work also includes assessing renewable-fuel production, supply chains, port infrastructure and bunkering requirements. (International Maritime Organization)

Regulatory uncertainty adds pressure

The delay surrounding the Net-Zero Framework has increased uncertainty for companies planning investments across the maritime fuel supply chain.

The proposed rules would apply to oceangoing vessels above 5,000 gross tons, which the IMO says account for more than 85% of international shipping emissions. Once adopted, the framework is expected to take effect after a 16-month period under the MARPOL process. (International Maritime Organization)

The economic component remains particularly important because it would place a price on greenhouse-gas emissions while providing incentives for cleaner energy use.

Governments are continuing to work through unresolved issues before the framework can move toward formal adoption.

Next IMO talks could shape the path to 2030

The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee held its 84th session in April-May 2026 and agreed to continue work through an intersessional working group before the next major committee meeting.

The IMO has scheduled further discussions ahead of MEPC 85, set for November 30-December 3, 2026. A second extraordinary MEPC session is scheduled for December 4, subject to confirmation at MEPC 85. (International Maritime Organization)

The timetable leaves the industry with a shrinking window to scale up alternative fuels, vessels and infrastructure before 2030.

For shipowners and fuel suppliers, the challenge is no longer simply whether low- and zero-emission technologies can be developed. The immediate question is whether regulation, financing, fuel availability and customer demand can expand quickly enough to support widespread commercial deployment.

title: Shipping’s Transition Being Hampered By Policy Uncertainty, Yet Industry Progress Continues
summary: Shipping’s lobby groups again attribute slow decarbonization to "policy uncertainty," conveniently deflecting from the industry's own inertia towards tangible emissions reductions. Despite the talk of 2030 zero-emission fuel targets, many operators persist with excessive HFO consumption, directly increasing carbon intensity and exposure to FuelEU Maritime penalties. Such reports often deflect from the urgent need for immediate, drastic cuts in CO2, rather than waiting for hypothetical future fuels.
content:
The shipping industry is at greater risk than ever of missing its 2030 zero-emission fuel targets, due in large part to the regulatory uncertainty of the last 12 months, according to a new report.

Launched today at New York Climate Week, the fifth edition of the ‘Climate action in shipping: Progress towards shipping’s 2030 breakthrough’ report tracks the sector’s advancement towards its climate target of having at least 5-10% of the fuel used in international shipping come from scalable zero-emission sources (SZEF) by 2030. This is the estimated level of SZEF uptake needed to meet the ambitions laid out in the 2023 International Maritime Organization (IMO) Greenhouse Gas Strategy, and ultimately, the industry’s entire 2050 net-zero goal.

The latest edition of the report reveals mixed progress towards that swiftly approaching target, with multiple indicators demonstrating the flow-on effects of economic and political upheaval, the crisis in Hormuz, energy security and supply chain concerns, and the regulatory uncertainty caused by the failure to adopt the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework (NZF) last year.

“Shipping’s energy transition is necessary and is going to happen. The obviously worsening impacts of climate change demand it. The 2030 breakthrough target was embraced by an industry that needs to start bringing tomorrow’s zero-emission fuels to market today if it is going to do its part,” said Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum. “While the geopolitical turmoil of the past year has frustrated this process, with the right policy push, accelerated industry action can still deliver on this crucial ambition. Adoption of the Net-Zero Framework at the IMO would allow that acceleration to begin in earnest.”

Across the five key ‘levers’ used to assess the industry’s progress (technology and supply, demand, finance, policy, and civil society), there have been multiple achievements. The past year has seen the world’s first ammonia bunkering and sea trials, a 53% increase in the number of ports offering methanol bunkering (19 to 29), a tripling of methanol-capable in-service tonnage (the largest single-year capability gain ever), and the global shipping finance portfolio’s greatest improvement in climate alignment on record.

“Shipping’s pathway to zero remains achievable, investable, and aligned with development goals. Positive progress in technology and zero-emission fuel supply is encouraging, but investment decisions cannot afford to wait,” said Dan Ioschpe, Climate High-Level Champion for COP30. “Demand for zero-emission shipping and financial flows directed toward zero-emission shipping are critical to accelerating the pace. Done right, climate action in shipping will increase competitiveness, improve energy security, and drive socio-economic development.”

Despite this positive progress, other key levers needed to reach the 2030 breakthrough target (particularly across demand, finance, and policy) have either stagnated or worsened since the last report. With demand signals weakened by the widespread ‘wait and see’ approach to global regulation, the order book has regressed (SZEF-capable vessels fell from 9.5% to 5.7% of total tonnage on order), and shipping-specific sustainable debt issuance decreased from $3.4 billion in 2024 to $3.0 billion in 2025.

“The failure to adopt the NZF was the single most transition-regressive event we’ve seen in the five years this report has been running,” said Dr Pinar Langer, research fellow at the UCL Energy Institute. “Reversing this momentum loss and securing regulatory certainty this year is therefore one of the most important next steps to give shipowners the confidence to order zero-emission vessels, lenders the incentive to invest in them, and charterers the impetus to pay for low-carbon shipping.”

The report makes multiple recommendations, including that the IMO adopt the NZF ‘as is’ at the upcoming session in December, as this will create the global policy clarity and direction the ecosystem urgently needs. It also stresses the growing importance of national and regional policies that underpin SZEF production to de-risk first-mover action, regardless of what happens next at the IMO.

2026 progress tracker

• Technology and SZEF supply – partially on track

• Demand – not on track

• Finance – not on track

• Policy – not on track

• Civil society – partially on track

Definitions

Scalable zero-emissions fuel (SZEF)

The report sets several key conditions for SZEF. These include the need for the fuels to be:

• scalable, such that the 200-300 million tonnes (Mt) of oil equivalent of current annual consumption can be matched in the foreseeable future;

• producible with greenhouse gas intensity reductions of 90-100% relative to incumbent fossil-based fuels on a full life cycle (well-to-wake) basis; and

• competitive in cost of production in the foreseeable future, assuming continued research and development and the adoption of viable policy support mechanisms.

title: Trump Takes Aim at Shipping’s Net-Zero Plan at UN
summary: President Donald Trump has reignited his opposition to the IMO's Net-Zero Framework, mischaracterizing it as a global carbon tax that would inflate shipping costs by up to 20%. This political pressure, including past threats of economic retaliation, targets an essential mechanism designed to progressively reduce global shipping's carbon intensity through compliance payments for high emitters. Such obstruction risks severely delaying critical decarbonization, thereby perpetuating the industry's reliance on high-carbon fuels and undermining urgent efforts to curb excessive emissions.
content:
President Donald Trump used his address to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday to renew his attack on the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework, accusing the UN shipping agency of attempting to impose a global carbon tax that would drive up transportation costs.

“Last year, my administration was forced to intervene to stop an obscure U.N. body, the International Maritime Organization, from secretly establishing a first-ever global carbon tax,” Trump said, claiming the measure would raise international shipping costs by “10 to 20% — and maybe more than that.”

“There is no global government,” Trump added. “And while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.”

The remarks elevate a fight that has been playing out at the IMO for more than a year and come as member states prepare for another attempt to finalize the framework in December.

The Trump administration played a major role in last year’s decision to postpone adoption. Ahead of the vote, U.S. officials threatened countries supporting the framework with measures including tariffs, visa restrictions, port fees and sanctions. The extraordinary Marine Environment Protection Committee session ultimately postponed adoption for one year following a 57-49 vote.

Trump had personally entered the fight a day earlier, declaring he was “outraged” over the proposed shipping carbon charge and calling on IMO member states to “vote NO”. His administration also warned at the time that countries backing the measure could face economic retaliation.

The United States has continued pushing for major changes as negotiations resumed this year.

The IMO Net-Zero Framework would combine progressively tighter greenhouse gas-intensity requirements for marine fuels with an economic mechanism requiring higher-emitting ships to make compliance payments while rewarding vessels using lower-emission fuels.

Trump’s description of the proposal as a “global carbon tax” reflects the language consistently used by his administration. Supporters of the framework describe it instead as a global greenhouse gas pricing mechanism tied to ships’ emissions performance.

Cost remains one of the central issues dividing IMO member states.

As gCaptain reported earlier this month, 38 countries speaking during the IMO’s latest technical negotiations explicitly supported retaining carbon pricing and the associated revenue mechanism, while 17 countries — many of them oil-producing states — opposed it over concerns about transportation costs and economic impacts.

The United States, Saudi Arabia, Liberia and several other countries have pushed for substantial changes or alternatives to parts of the existing framework. European countries, Pacific Island states and others have argued that weakening the pricing mechanism would undermine investment in alternative marine fuels and make the IMO’s long-term emissions targets harder to achieve.

The system is expected to generate roughly $10 billion to $15 billion annually, making both the size of the financial burden and how the money would ultimately be distributed among the most contentious issues still under negotiation.

Despite those divisions, the basic structure survived the IMO’s September negotiating session largely intact.

The debate has increasingly shifted toward whether the final rules will provide enough certainty for shipowners and fuel producers to make long-term investment decisions. The Getting to Zero Coalition warned earlier this month that thousands of new vessels will be ordered in the coming years, potentially locking in fuel and technology choices for decades.

The framework traces back to the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy, which calls for international shipping to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by or around 2050.

The next round of technical negotiations is scheduled for November 23-27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s MEPC 85 session from November 30 through December 3.

The Net-Zero Framework is then expected to return for possible adoption at an extraordinary MEPC session on December 4.

Trump’s comments at the UN leave little doubt that Washington intends to remain firmly opposed as that vote approaches.

The Getting to Zero Coalition is a powerful alliance of more than 200 organisations (including over 180 private companies) within the maritime, energy, infrastructure, and finance sectors. title: GCMD and Equinor partner to advance alternative fuel- and carbon value chains
summary: The Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Equinor have announced a five-year "Impact partnership" to "advance alternative fuel and carbon value chains," a common industry euphemism for future promises. While touting expertise in "real-world pilots" and "low-carbon solutions," the announcement offers no immediate, concrete reductions in current fleet carbon intensity or HFO consumption. dirtiestships.com awaits actual data on how this partnership will prevent FuelEU Maritime fines for Equinor's chartered fleet, rather than merely discussing future fuel options.
content:
The Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Equinor today announced a five-year Impact partnership.

The partnership brings together GCMD’s capabilities in conducting real-world maritime pilots with Equinor’s experience as a charterer, energy provider and developer of low-carbon solutions.

Together, the organisations will leverage their complementary expertise to help address technical and operational gaps in scaling alternative marine fuels and supporting the development and uptake of other maritime decarbonisation solutions.

Advancing the safe deployment and assurance of alternative marine fuels

GCMD’s work on alternative fuels, including biofuels, ammonia and methanol, focuses on two critical aspects of deployment: operational safety and robust monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV). Its pilots and studies are generating operational data to support safe bunkering and handling of these fuels. At the same time, its assurance work seeks to strengthen confidence in quantity, quality and GHG emissions abatement.

Equinor brings extensive experience as a vessel charterer and marine fuel supplier. This includes chartering dual-fuel LNG, LPG and methanol tankers, testing and using biofuels and supplying methanol to the maritime sector. Equinor is also piloting the use and supply of ammonia as a marine fuel, contributing to the development of associated safety, regulatory and bunkering arrangements.

Combining these perspectives can help address practical barriers to alternative fuels deployment while strengthening assurance across emerging marine fuel value chains.

Supporting the uptake of maritime decarbonisation solutions

Beyond alternative fuels, GCMD is working to accelerate the adoption of solutions that can reduce emissions from the existing fleet, including energy efficiency technologies (EETs) and onboard carbon capture and storage (OCCS).

GCMD’s work on EETs includes quantifying real-world fuel savings from technologies such as wind-assisted propulsion systems and developing financing mechanisms to scale their adoption. In OCCS, Project CAPTURED demonstrated an end-to-end value chain for onboard captured and liquefied CO₂, generating evidence that contributed to the recognition of captured CO2 under the EU ETS and in-principle support at the IMO for recognising carbon mineralisation as permanent storage.

Equinor brings decades of experience in offshore CO₂ storage, including its role in the development and operation of Northern Lights, the world’s first cross-border CO2 transport and storage facility, where liquefied CO₂ is transported by ship to an onshore receiving terminal before it is sent by pipeline for permanent geological storage beneath the North Sea.

Through the partnership, GCMD and Equinor will explore opportunities to combine their respective capabilities and experience to support the deployment and scaling of maritime decarbonisation solutions.

We are excited about what this partnership with Equinor can unlock. Shipping’s transition will require a portfolio of decarbonisation solutions, and moving them from promising concepts and demonstrations to adoption at scale requires us to address the practical barriers that remain. GCMD is proud to join forces with Equinor to generate the operational evidence needed to close these gaps and build confidence in solutions that can deliver meaningful emissions reductions.

Professor Lynn Loo, CEO, GCMD

The maritime energy transition requires collaboration across industries and value chains, and we’re excited to join GCMD as an Impact Partner. Equinor brings expertise and practical experience from across the energy and maritime sectors, and we look forward to working with and learning from other industry partners. Together, we can help address barriers, improve understanding of emerging solutions and support progress towards lower-emission shipping.

Anne Mai Hatlem, Senior Vice President, Marketing, Midstream & Processing (MMP), Equinor

Source: Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD)

title: Autonomous vessels, cleaner fuels, new careers: Inside Singapore’s plan to keep its edge in shipping
summary: Singapore promotes its "plan to keep its edge" with autonomous vessels and "cleaner fuels," yet this narrative lacks any specific, quantifiable commitments to significantly reduce its fleet's carbon intensity. Despite being the world's leading bunkering hub, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) offers no concrete targets to curb the excessive HFO consumption from the 1,000 ships daily in its waters. Without transparent metrics for CO2 emissions per tonne-mile or clear penalties for vessels exceeding their CII rating, these "sustainability" claims remain typical greenwashing.
content:
Think about the things that you use every day – your smartphone, the coffee beans that go into your morning brew, or the chair that you are sitting on. Chances are, they travelled thousands of miles by sea before reaching Singapore.

More than 80 per cent of the world’s goods are transported by sea, making the maritime industry the backbone of global trade. And Singapore sits at the heart of this ecosystem. It is the world’s leading container transshipment and bunkering – or vessel-fuelling – hub.

At any given time, about 1,000 ships are in Singapore’s waters, carrying essential goods such as food, fuel and construction materials.

Ng Yi Han, chief transformation officer and senior director for Innovation, Technology and Talent Development at the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), shares: “Many people may not realise this, but the maritime industry plays an outsized role, especially in Singapore, where we are a major global supply chain hub.”

Watch to find out more about the maritime industry.

Singapore’s influence extends well beyond its shores. It is home to one of the world’s busiest ports and punches above its weight in global maritime trade. Its strategic location, world-class port infrastructure, global connectivity, trusted institutions and deep ecosystem of maritime services have made it a key node of global commerce.

Keeping everyday life moving

As a member of the Council of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) – the United Nations agency responsible for regulating international shipping – Singapore actively supports the IMO in shaping global standards and policies that govern the industry.

For all its importance, the maritime sector often operates out of the public spotlight. Many see only the ships and ports, not the diverse careers behind them – from technology and sustainability to policy, logistics and global trade.

“People usually don’t see the maritime industry working quietly behind the scenes 24/7,” says Ng. “The average Singaporean doesn’t realise that when they do their groceries at the supermarket, these goods are actually brought to Singapore by ships from all over the world.”

When these supply chains are disrupted, the effects can be felt across the economy through shortages, delays and rising costs.

Ng experienced this first-hand. When the Covid-19 pandemic struck, he watched as port congestion and crew shortages cascaded into global supply chain disruptions. This led to emptied supermarket shelves and drove up prices worldwide.

“When the maritime industry is under stress, the ripple effects spread far beyond the ports, and everyone feels it,” he recalls.

Despite the industry’s significance, maritime may not always be top of mind for fresh graduates or professionals considering a career switch.

“Many people think that the maritime industry is all about the vessels and operating the vessels as a seafarer, but it goes beyond that,” says Ng.

While seafarers remain a vital part of the workforce, today’s maritime industry offers opportunities across commercial, engineering and technology functions. Roles in the industry range from monitoring global trade flows and developing cleaner fuels, to applying digital tools and artificial intelligence to optimise maritime operations.

“In order for the maritime industry to work well and efficiently, we do need a diverse workforce,” says Ng.

“A workforce not just in technical roles such as seafaring and operational roles, but also in commercial and technology-related roles as well.”

When ports become innovation hubs

Another common misconception is that maritime is a traditional industry with little room for innovation. In reality, technologies are rapidly reshaping ports, ships and global supply chains.

“The industry is moving towards using technology, AI and automation to drive progress. These tools are going to play an important role in not just shipping itself but also in the global supply chain. And what this means is that ports are also going to be increasingly automated,” says Ng.

At PSA, port operations are coordinated from shore-based operation centres, where equipment can be monitored and even operated remotely with a high degree of efficiency.

At Seatrium, their Yard Of The Future initiative uses digital twins of its global shipyards, allowing engineers to detect anomalies on digital dashboards before they become real-world problems.

The future could see even larger changes. MPA and PSA are inviting proposals to develop and test autonomous inter-gateway container feeder vessel operations within Singapore’s port.

These innovations create new career opportunities in areas such as remote vessel monitoring and operations, autonomous systems engineering, maritime data analytics and specialised technical maintenance.

Alongside digitalisation and automation, sustainability has become a major priority for the maritime sector. International shipping accounts for around 3 per cent of global carbon emissions.

To reduce their environmental footprint, international shipping is exploring cleaner energy sources such as biofuels, methanol and ammonia, while Singapore is also working towards electrifying local harbour crafts.

To support the transition, a $100m Maritime Singapore Green Initiative (MSGI) was launched in 2011 to promote clean and green shipping in Singapore, and by 2030, all new harbour craft in Singapore’s waters must operate on low-carbon energy solutions.

Singapore is also accelerating efforts on the use of biofuels and establishing methanol and ammonia bunkering at scale, which will reduce the carbon footprint of ships.

New pathways into maritime careers

As maritime evolves, so too must its workforce. MPA is working closely with educational institutions to build a strong talent pipeline.

“We work with the universities, the polytechnics, as well as ITE on the various maritime careers,” says Ng. “We support them in reviewing some of their maritime-related curriculum.”

New programmes are also being introduced to broaden the pathways into the sector. These include an Industry Graduate Diploma in Maritime at Singapore Management University and a master’s-level vessel management programme at the Singapore Institute of Technology.

They add to existing maritime programmes, including master’s-level courses in Maritime Studies at Nanyang Technological University (NTU) and Maritime Technology Management at the National University of Singapore, as well as undergraduate and polytechnic programmes at NTU and the Singapore Maritime Academy at Singapore Polytechnic.

But a maritime qualification is not the only way into the industry. Ng himself came from a computer engineering background and started out as a research and development executive. Drawn to maritime by the opportunities to apply technology and innovation, he has since risen through the ranks over more than 20 years and now helps shape how the industry evolves.

“What is most important is really to have the passion to gain more exposure to the industry,” he says. “We welcome students from non-maritime disciplines because a lot of the technologies and solutions come from other domains and disciplines.”

The industry also welcomes mid-career professionals from adjacent sectors such as logistics, commodities and trading. Career conversion programmes can help these professionals acquire the skills needed to transition into maritime roles.

“It will be very useful if the person is a problem solver, and is able to work with uncertainties or challenges,” Ng says. “Maritime is also a very international industry, so the ability to engage different cultures and understand different perspectives is important.”

title: How three wars are crowding out the challenges that will actually define the next decade
summary: While geopolitical conflicts dominate headlines, the shipping industry's critical decarbonization targets are quietly being missed amidst the distraction. This allows many vessels to continue with excessive HFO usage, maintaining high carbon intensity and delaying vital investments in alternative fuels. Such complacency guarantees future FuelEU Maritime fines and exposes the industry's persistent greenwashing over genuine emissions reduction efforts.
content:
Punit Oza from Maritime NXT on risks that come from crisis distraction, a big topic up for discussion at Thursday’s Splash Singapore conference.

Since early 2026 the world’s attention — and its risk desks, insurance markets, and naval assets — have been consumed by three overlapping conflicts. The Russia-Ukraine war has ground into its fifth year with no ceasefire in sight, Russian drone and missile barrages continuing even as Ukraine’s counter-strikes hit deep into Russian energy infrastructure. The Iran war that erupted in February 2026 has lurched through ceasefire, memorandum, collapse, and resumption, with Hormuz transits still running well below pre-war averages and Brent crude gyrating on every headline out of Islamabad or Tehran. And the Red Sea, which briefly reopened after the Gaza ceasefire, has seen Houthi attacks resume, pushing a meaningful share of Asia-Europe container and tanker traffic back around the Cape of Good Hope.

Each of these crises deserves the attention it gets. Seafarers have died. Cargo has been lost. War-risk premiums have reshaped freight economics overnight. But there is a cost to living permanently in crisis mode: the slower-moving, more consequential shifts reshaping trade, energy, and demography get pushed to the bottom of the agenda — right when decisions taken now will compound for decades.

As I often frame it to my students and clients: a shipowner who only reads the weather report in front of the bow will eventually be surprised by the current underneath the keel. The conflicts are the weather. Climate transition, decarbonization, demographic imbalance, and the reordering of soft power are the current.

Climate change and decarbonisation: quietly missing its own deadline

IMO’s 2023 GHG strategy and the more recent Net-Zero Framework set a trajectory toward net-zero shipping by around mid-century, with interim checkpoints this decade. That trajectory assumed sustained capital flow into alternative fuels, port infrastructure, and fleet renewal. Instead, capital and attention have been diverted toward war-risk cover, convoy escorts, rerouting costs, and bunker price volatility driven by Gulf tensions.

The irony is sharp: every extra week a VLCC spends going around the Cape instead of through the Red Sea burns more fuel and emits more carbon than the direct route — the conflicts are making decarbonization arithmetic harder even as they dominate the news cycle that should be driving decarbonization policy. Green corridors, ammonia and methanol bunkering infrastructure, and newbuild ordering for alternative-fuel tonnage all require long investment horizons and calm capital markets. Geopolitical volatility is the natural enemy of that kind of patient investment.

Demographic imbalance: shipping’s quiet manpower crisis

While headlines track troop movements, a different kind of shortage is building: seafarers. The traditional labour-supplying nations — the Philippines, India, Indonesia, China — face their own demographic transitions, rising domestic wage expectations, and competition from shore-based industries. Meanwhile, officer shortages are already visible in tanker and gas segments, and they will worsen as an aging cohort of experienced masters and chief engineers retires faster than training pipelines can replace them.

This is not a problem conflict created, but conflict has made it worse in a specific way: war-risk transits through the Red Sea and the Gulf have made seafaring measurably more dangerous again, at exactly the moment the industry needs to make the profession more attractive, not less. Crew welfare, hazard pay, and safe-passage guarantees — issues I engage with directly through my work on maritime connectivity and crew welfare technology — deserve as much strategic bandwidth as any war-risk clause, but rarely get it.

China’s soft power: expanding while the West looks elsewhere

Perhaps the most underappreciated shift of the past two years is how much diplomatic and commercial ground China — and to a striking degree, Pakistan as a mediator in the Iran conflict — has covered while Western attention was fixed on Ukraine, Iran, and the Red Sea. Beijing’s involvement was reportedly a factor in nudging Tehran toward the April 2026 ceasefire, a reminder that Chinese leverage in the Gulf now extends well beyond oil purchases into active crisis diplomacy. The Belt and Road Initiative continues to knit together port, rail, and energy infrastructure across the Global South largely without competing Western financing on offer.

For shipping, this matters directly. Port ownership, terminal concessions, and shipbuilding capacity are shifting toward Chinese state and private entities across Africa, South Asia, and Latin America, often as the only credible capital available. Soft power built through infrastructure, financing, and mediation does not show up in a single dramatic headline — it accumulates. By the time it is visible, the map has already changed.

The Asia and Global South pivot: the structural story underneath the noise

Strip away the conflict-driven volatility and a clear structural trend remains: trade gravity continues shifting toward intra-Asia and Global South corridors. Intra-Asian trade volumes, South-South trade flows, and manufacturing relocation out of China into Vietnam, India, Bangladesh, and increasingly parts of Africa are reshaping the map of who ships what, to whom, and through which chokepoints.

Ironically, the very conflicts distracting policymakers are accelerating this pivot. Red Sea disruption has made European buyers reconsider sourcing distance and lead times, favouring nearer, less chokepoint-dependent supply chains. Hormuz volatility has pushed Gulf energy buyers in Asia to diversify sourcing toward the Americas and West Africa. Sanctions on Russian crude have rerouted tanker flows toward India and China at discounted rates, entrenching new trading relationships that will outlast the sanctions themselves. Every disruption is, in effect, redrawing trade lanes in favour of the Global South’s growing consumption base and away from the traditional West-centric axis.

The strategic mindset shipping needs now

None of this argues for ignoring the wars. War risk must be priced, routes must be planned, and crews must be protected — today, not eventually. But the leaders who will be best positioned in 2030 are the ones treating today’s crises and tomorrow’s structural shifts as a single strategic picture, not two separate inboxes.

This is precisely the case for what I call the Chief Geostrategic Officer mindset: maritime and trade leaders cannot simply manage inward-facing operational risk while conflict dominates the horizon. They must simultaneously read the slower currents — decarbonisation deadlines that don’t pause for wars, a workforce that is aging out faster than it is being replenished, a soft-power map being redrawn quietly, and a trade axis tilting decisively toward Asia and the Global South.

The conflicts will eventually settle, as conflicts do. The current underneath will keep moving regardless. The question worth asking in every boardroom and bridge is not only “how do we get through this crisis” but “what did we fail to build while we were looking at it.”

title: BetterSea and GTT Marine Partner to Bring FuelEU Trading and Pooling to Vesper Insights
summary: BetterSea and GTT Marine are partnering to offer a FuelEU Maritime compliance platform, enabling shipping companies to trade and pool emission allowances. This integration primarily facilitates financial management of FuelEU obligations, allowing companies to buy and sell credits rather than mandating direct emissions reductions. dirtiestships.com maintains that true decarbonization requires verifiable cuts in HFO consumption and carbon intensity, not just sophisticated compliance trading mechanisms.
content:
BetterSea, provider of a leading FuelEU compliance platform and marketplace, and GTT Marine, a business unit of the GTT Group, today announced a white-label integration partnership to accelerate FuelEU Maritime compliance for shipping companies.

Under the partnership, GTT Marine will integrate BetterSea’s platform into its own Vesper Insights platform offering, enabling GTT Marine customers and platform users to seamlessly execute FuelEU trading and pooling end-to-end, directly from the Vesper Insights platform. Through this white-label integration, customers will gain access to BetterSea’s full FuelEU infrastructure, including marketplace access, simulation tools, pooling and post-trade workflows, as well as streamlined Thetis reporting capabilities, all within the Vesper Insights environment. This creates a uniquely aligned offering for customers seeking a single, trusted route to FuelEU compliance and execution.

As FuelEU Maritime moves into operational reality, shipping companies need more than visibility into compliance exposure. They need the ability to assess options, execute transactions, and complete workflows reliably and at scale. The BetterSea-GTT Marine partnership addresses that need by combining BetterSea’s execution-ready FuelEU platform with GTT Marine strong position in vessel performance and maritime innovation.

Delivering tangible value to clients

Through the BetterSea-GTT Marine partnership, customers will gain:

· seamless access to FuelEU trading and pooling execution directly within GTT Marine Vesper Insights platform

· access to BetterSea’s FuelEU marketplace and daily FuelEU surplus index

· simulation tools to compare compliance pathways across different regulations and evaluate cost exposure

· pooling and post-trade workflows supported by standardized legal and financial structures

· pool tracking and Thetis reporting capabilities to support the full FuelEU execution process

· fully streamlined and connected route to end-to-end FuelEU compliance

The result is a more practical, scalable, and execution-focused compliance experience for shipowners, operators, and charterers navigating FuelEU Maritime.

“This partnership with GTT Marine marks an important step in our mission to make FuelEU compliance and pooling easier to access and execute, while underlining BetterSea’s position as the market leading FuelEU marketplace. By embedding our platform into GTT Marine Vesper Insights offering, we are giving customers a seamless and efficient path from compliance understanding to full trading and pooling execution, all within an environment they already know and use.” Maximilian Schroer, Co-CEO, BetterSea

“At GTT Marine, we are committed to equipping our customers with practical and high-value solutions for the decarbonisation transition. Through this partnership with BetterSea, we can offer our users direct access to a complete FuelEU execution framework, from simulation to trading, pooling, and reporting, directly via our platform.” Christian Treu, VP Revenue, GTT Marine

A shared commitment to practical decarbonisation

FuelEU Maritime introduced new commercial, operational, and regulatory complexity for shipping companies. Addressing it effectively requires more than fragmented tools or standalone advisory support. It requires a connected infrastructure for compliance understanding, decision-making, cross-party alignment, execution, and reporting.

The latest partnership between BetterSea and GTT Marine reflects that approach. By bringing together complementary capabilities in maritime technology and FuelEU execution, the two companies are enabling a more intelligent, standardized, and scalable pathway to compliance.

title: ABB brings UK’s first high-voltage multi-berth shore power system into service in Portsmouth International Port
summary: Portsmouth International Port has commissioned the UK's first high-voltage multi-berth shore power, claiming to avoid 20,000 tonnes CO2e annually from 2027. While ferries and cruise ships like Virgin Voyages' *Valiant Lady* can now plug in, this only mitigates emissions at berth, not addressing their overall carbon intensity (CII) or HFO usage during transit. The port's "net zero by 2035" ambition remains highly questionable without mandating clean fuels or comprehensive decarbonization across all vessel operations, not just shore power connections.
content:
ABB shore power solution allows ferries and cruise ships alongside the port’s three busiest berths to turn off their engines and plug into the local power grid. Following extensive testing of the system by the Brittany Ferries vessels Saint Malo and Guillaume de Normandie, Virgin Voyages' Valiant Lady became the first commercial cruise ship to plug in at the terminal during August 20261.

Portsmouth International Port estimates that, as well as improving air quality and reducing noise, shore power will avoid carbon dioxide equivalent emissions (CO2e) from ship calls of around 20,000 tonnes2 each year from 2027 onward.

“We are the first port in the country to have high-voltage multi-berth, multi-user, multi-frequency shore power connections,” said Mike Sellers, Port Director of Portsmouth International Port. “We'll be able to connect up to three vessels at the same time, and that will help meet our objectives of being net zero by 2035, and the first zero emission port in the UK by 2050.”

The UK’s largest municipal port, Portsmouth offers more ferry routes than any other in the nation. Also known for its rich naval history, ecological importance and leisure, Portsmouth welcomed calls from a record 94 scheduled cruise ships in 2025.

“I want to congratulate everyone involved in this huge undertaking” said Councilor Steve Pitt, Leader of Portsmouth City Council. “The system sets Portsmouth apart in the UK cruise and ferry market, cements our sustainability ambitions, and contributes to our ongoing commitment to the health of people across the city.”

The shore connection initiative comes under the port’s ‘Sea Change’ project – itself part of the UK Government-funded Zero Emissions Vessels and Infrastructure (ZEVI) competition which was delivered in partnership with Innovate UK. Sea Change includes a plan for shore power to support the charging of two new hybrid-LNG ferries that will enter and leave the port under 100 percent renewable electric power.

As the UK’s largest shore power installation to date, the system’s impact on ship emissions will be discernible as well as measurable, at a time when the UK Chamber of Shipping acknowledges the nation’s ports lag behind others in adopting shore power3.

ABB looked after the whole electrical infrastructure needed for the shore power for ferries and for the cruise ships. It is also contracted to provide shore connection service and remote support across all three berths.

The installation offers other UK port operators an up-close insight into the comprehensive shore power competence that ABB’s Marine & Ports division can provide as part of its strategy to support maritime decarbonization across multiple vessel requirements. It has been designed to connect ships at 11 kV 50 hertz, 11 kV 60 hertz, and also at 6.6 kV 50 hertz and 6.6 kV 60 hertz.

Portsmouth also offers the latest example of a shore power solution featuring the ‘e-house’, where the main onshore power supply equipment is installed in containers on a prefabricated basis by ABB for easy delivery into the port. Other ABB problem-solving initiatives included the location of shore connection transformers under terminal linkspans, away from operating areas where space is at a premium

Where cruise ships feature plug-in points in non-standard locations, a solution has also been found to cover requirements along Berth No.2, through acquisition of a remotely operated vehicle with its own cable management system.

“This is a very important project for ABB, as the largest shore power project in the UK and as a new example of the multi-berth solutions major ports need to meet their ambitions on decarbonization,” said Marcus Martelin, Head of Decarbonization Services, ABB’s Marine & Ports division. “It has been a privilege to fulfil our obligations as a technology provider for this UK Government-funded project and consolidate our reputation as a trusted provider of shore connection capabilities for cleaner port operations. This is a pivotal step in the UK’s journey towards a greener maritime future.”
